glossary.explanation: The official Chinese and Russian position on how the war should be understood, stressing the decisive roles of China and the USSR and the legitimacy of the postwar tribunals.
In Chinese Party usage, a label for interpretations seen as denying or distorting official accounts of history.
The system of institutions and norms built after 1945, centred on the United Nations and the UN Charter.

t: Learning from history, committed to rejuvenation
zh: 镜鉴历史 矢志复兴
authors: Institute of Military Political Work Research, Academy of Military Sciences
paras: Written for the 80th anniversary of victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War, this commentary by a research institute of the Academy of Military Sciences asks what that war should teach China today. It opens with Xi Jinping's article in Rossiyskaya Gazeta during his May 2025 visit to Russia. The authors argue that the lessons of the war must be absorbed to keep the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation on course.

The piece has three parts. The first describes the suffering inflicted by Japan's invasion, citing figures on casualties, destroyed industry, economic loss and cultural plunder. The second sets out how the victory, in the authors' account, opened the way to national rejuvenation. The third draws four present-day lessons on Party leadership, the people, national security and world peace.

In the second part the authors present five legacies of the war. It tempered the Communist Party into a mature leading force, with Mao Zedong Thought established and the Yan'an rectification campaign strengthening Party building. It awakened the whole nation, and it forged a people's army rooted in the masses through guerrilla warfare. It also produced the great spirit of resistance and restored China's standing as a major power, including its role in founding the United Nations. The authors cite casualties of more than 35 million Chinese soldiers and civilians and direct economic losses of 100 billion US dollars.

The lessons for today follow from this. The authors call for stronger Party leadership and full and rigorous self-governance of the Party, and for a people-centred approach, since the people are described as the creators of history. They urge stronger strategic capacity to defend sovereignty and security, summed up as 'only those able to fight can stop war', and say the military must be ready to win when called on. They also call for upholding a correct view of the Second World War, the postwar order and the UN Charter, and for building a community with a shared future for mankind. Remembering history, they say, is meant to cherish peace and not to perpetuate hatred. Read the original if you want an example of how a military-affiliated body in Qiushi ties the war's memory to Party building, defence preparedness and foreign-policy themes.
quoteEn: The great spirit of resistance is the most precious spiritual legacy the War of Resistance left us, and a powerful driving force for the Chinese nation as it moves towards the future and towards rejuvenation.
quoteZh: 伟大抗战精神是抗日战争留给我们最宝贵的精神财富，是中华民族走向未来、走向复兴的强大动力。

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.literal: great revival of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central official goal of the Communist Party, presented as restoring China's strength and international standing after the 'century of humiliation' that began in 1840.

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.explanation: Official slogan, prominent since 2012, for tightening Party discipline, anti-corruption work and cadre management.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's foreign-policy concept of a world built on cooperation and shared interests, promoted since around 2013.
A campaign of ideological education and discipline within the Party in 1942–45, which consolidated Mao Zedong's leadership and line.

glossary.literal: taking the people as the centre
glossary.explanation: An official principle that development and governance should serve the people's interests and rely on them.

t: China's War of Resistance changed the course of the world anti-fascist war
zh: 中国抗战改变世界反法西斯战争走向
paras: This short commentary, published in the China Social Sciences Today in May 2025, argues that the 14-year Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression was not only a part of the world anti-fascist war but altered its course. Wang Fengqing contends that China's resistance changed the fate of the Chinese nation and made an immeasurable contribution to final victory.

The article is organised in three parts. It first treats China as the earliest and longest-fighting anti-fascist country, then China's role in advocating and promoting a world anti-fascist alliance, and finally China's support for the Soviet–German and Pacific theatres.

Wang first stresses timing and scale. Beginning with the Mukden Incident of 1931, China fought alone for eight years before war broke out in Europe and for over ten before the Pacific War. The author cites over 200 major battles, the elimination of more than 1.5 million Japanese troops, and Chinese casualties above 21 million. Second, Wang credits the Communist Party with proposing a united front from 1933 and with calling for an international one, culminating in the Declaration by United Nations of 1 January 1942. Third, Wang argues that, because Japan's northward and southward expansion both required first conquering China, tying down its main forces prevented an attack on the Soviet Far East and weakened Japan against US forces in the Pacific. Wang cites Stalin on avoiding a two-front war.

Wang concludes that China's sacrifice and tenacity broke Japanese fascism's strategic plans and made China one of the decisive factors in the anti-fascist victory, citing Mao Zedong's remark that the war was a matter for the world, not China alone. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese academic commentary in 2025 presents China's wartime role within the global anti-fascist struggle.
quoteEn: The state of the Chinese theatre played a pivotal role in how Japan formulated and carried out its "northward" and "southward" advance policies.
quoteZh: 中国战场状况如何，对日本“北进”“南进”政策的制定和实施起着举足轻重的作用。

glossary.explanation: The wartime alliance policy, advanced by the Chinese Communist Party, of cooperating with the Nationalists and other forces against Japan. The article also extends the idea to an international anti-fascist front.
The Japanese military's staged attack and occupation of Manchuria beginning on 18 September 1931. Chinese historiography treats it as the start of the 14-year war of resistance.
A document signed in Washington on 1 January 1942 by 26 Allied states pledging joint war effort against the Axis powers.

t: Resolutely upholding the post-war international order
zh: 坚决维护战后国际秩序
paras: Writing in the year of the 80th anniversary of victory in the World Anti-Fascist War and of the founding of the United Nations, Wu Zhicheng argues that the post-war international order must be firmly defended against unilateralism and hegemonic bullying. The commentary takes as its starting point Xi Jinping's 7 May 2025 signed article in Rossiyskaya Gazeta, "Draw on History and Create the Future Together", and presents itself as an exposition of its significance. Wu holds that humanity again stands at a crossroads between unity and division, dialogue and confrontation, win-win and zero-sum outcomes.

The piece is organised in four parts. It first sets out the historical and legal basis of the post-war order, then its political and economic content, then its present-day value, and finally China's role in defending it. Wu draws on the UN Charter, the Cairo Declaration, the Potsdam Proclamation, the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials and the Yalta system, and refers to the IMF, World Bank and WTO as the economic pillars.

Wu contends that the order rests on firm legal foundations and that China and the Soviet Union, as the main Asian and European theatres of the war, earned their permanent Security Council seats through their contribution. The order is imperfect, Wu says, but because it is rule-based, fairness-oriented and aimed at shared gains it should not be discarded or rebuilt from scratch. Wu says that certain countries' tariffs, export controls and sanctions bypassing the Security Council violate the Charter and WTO rules, and the commentary names the United States as the order's greatest beneficiary now turning against it. Defending the order is tied to peace and development, the authority of the UN, the future of multilateralism and the democratisation of international relations.

On China's role, Wu calls for upholding the UN-centred system, promoting equal and orderly multipolarity and inclusive economic globalisation, and strengthening the voice of developing countries through the WTO, BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation. The commentary also states that Taiwan's return to China is part of the war's outcome and the post-war order, citing the Cairo Declaration, the Potsdam Proclamation and UN General Assembly Resolution 2758, and that China will be unified. Read the original if you want a concise example of how a Central Party School scholar frames the post-war order, multilateralism and Taiwan in official discourse in 2025.
quoteEn: The current international order is also imperfect, but as long as it is rule-based, fairness-oriented and aimed at win-win outcomes, it cannot be casually abandoned, still less torn down and rebuilt from scratch.
quoteZh: 现行国际秩序也不完美，但只要它以规则为基础，以公平为导向，以共赢为目标，就不能随意被舍弃，更容不得推倒重来。

glossary.explanation: The idea that world power should be spread among several centres rather than dominated by one state. Official texts qualify it as 'equal and orderly'.
An official Chinese formulation calling for equality of all states, joint rule-making and opposition to hegemony in world affairs.

t: Promoting the correct view of the history of the Second World War
zh: 弘扬正确二战史观
paras: Writing in Guangming Daily on 15 May 2025, Liu Guangming and Peng Chunlin respond to Xi Jinping's call, made during his state visit to Russia for the 80th anniversary of victory in the Soviet Great Patriotic War, to "uphold" and "jointly promote" a correct view of the history of the Second World War. The commentary argues that this view matters for remembering history, for shared development and for defending international fairness and justice, and that it should be promoted actively.

The piece has three parts. The first sets out why the correct view matters now. The second defines its essential content. The third proposes how to promote it. The authors set this against what they call unilateralism and hegemonic bullying, and against attempts to make war history serve geopolitical struggle.

The authors say the correct view is, in essence, historical materialism and a "grand view of history". They make three claims. First, the world's peoples, including the Chinese and Soviet peoples, are the historical subject of the victory. Second, the record is established by data: the authors cite figures on Japanese troops tied down in China, over 1.5 million Japanese killed, wounded or captured, and 35 million Chinese military and civilian casualties. From these they conclude that China was the main Asian theatre and a "mainstay" of the war against Japan. Third, the view rests on a shared-destiny outlook. They describe the opposing, "erroneous" view as Western-centrism and a variant of social Darwinism and imperialism. In their account it filters the war's history to suit national interest and geopolitics, and it underplays the Chinese and Soviet contributions.

For promotion, the authors call for an international united front of opinion against glorifying Nazism, neo-Nazism and the revival of militarism, and for peace education. They also call for more research on Nazi and Japanese war crimes, for commemorations at key sites, and for studying Xi's statements within a Marxist historical-materialist framework. They link remembrance to a community with a shared future for mankind and the three global initiatives, to defending the postwar order and the UN, and to a security path of dialogue, partnership without alliance, and win-win outcomes. Read the original if you want an example of how official Chinese commentary framed the history of the war and its contemporary uses in 2025.
quoteEn: Behind a view of history lie views of morality and values.
quoteZh: 历史观的背后是道义观、价值观。

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A concept associated with Xi Jinping since around 2012. It presents the world's countries as sharing common interests and a common destiny, and it underpins Chinese foreign-policy language.
The Global Development Initiative, the Global Security Initiative and the Global Civilization Initiative, put forward by Xi Jinping between 2021 and 2023.

The Marxist theory that material production and social relations drive historical development, and that the people are the creators of history. Chinese official writing treats it as the basis for judging historical questions.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: A full review of how Western discourse positions China's War of Resistance against Japan
zh: 全面检视西方话语下的中国抗战定位
paras: Writing in a Chinese Social Sciences Today piece of May 2025, Liu argues that Western scholarship still systematically misplaces China's War of Resistance against Japan, despite recent shifts such as Rana Mitter's China's Forgotten Ally and Hans van de Ven's call to put China's experience into the concept of the Second World War. Liu holds that Chinese scholars should critically review this literature and build their own theoretical system for the war, one that can win global recognition.

The commentary has three parts. It first lists four biases in Western accounts, then explains their political and academic causes, and finally proposes a shift from being defined by others to defining oneself.

Liu identifies the biases as the marginalisation of the Eastern theatre, the reduction of China's war to attrition or a mere "tripwire", a failure to grasp the war as a whole and the nature of the "people's war", and the exaggeration of foreign aid. Cited authors include William Hill, Gerhard Weinberg, Anthony Kubek and Rana Mitter. Liu traces these biases to Cold War thinking and ideological prejudice, to Western-centrism (including John Keegan's "peripheral theatre" and the Fairbank "impact–response" model), and to selective use of archives, though newly opened Chinese sources such as the Chiang Kai-shek diaries have helped.

Liu calls for digital document platforms, transnational research communities and an independent body of knowledge on the war. As a first step Liu proposes a "rejuvenation paradigm", guided by historical materialism, rooted in Chinese historiography and centred on the Communist Party's leadership of national rejuvenation. Liu also wants China's war placed within global anti-fascist, anti-imperialist and anti-colonial narratives. Read the original if you want a concise Chinese academic critique of Western historiography on the Sino-Japanese war and the case for a self-defined research paradigm.
quoteEn: The struggle over historical discourse power is in essence a contest of the capacity for civilizational narrative.
quoteZh: 历史话语权的争夺本质上是文明叙事能力的较量。

glossary.explanation: A research framework the author proposes for studying the War of Resistance. It combines historical materialism, Chinese historiographical traditions and the narrative of national rejuvenation under Communist Party leadership.
A concept associated with Mao Zedong's strategy of mobilising the broad population for armed struggle. The author says Western scholars wrongly reduce it to a Communist political tactic.
A term in current Chinese academic policy for building Chinese-originated theories and concepts rather than relying on Western ones.

t: The "Chinese National Liberation Vanguard" before and after the outbreak of the all-out War of Resistance
zh: 全民族抗战爆发前后的“中华民族解放先锋队”
paras: This short historical piece, published in Guangming Daily in May 2025, examines the Chinese National Liberation Vanguard (known by its Chinese abbreviation, Minxian dui), a youth organisation born in the December Ninth Movement of 1935. Wang Jianwei argues that the Communist Party used it as its basic organisational form to reverse its unfavourable position in youth work after the failure of the Great Revolution. In the author's account, it mobilised young people as a vanguard force, helped the Party organisation grow and drew youth into the national War of Resistance.

The article follows the organisation in three stages. It first covers the formation of the vanguard from the southward propaganda corps of early 1936 and its training, publicity and recruitment work through that year. It then turns to the Party's leadership and the organisation's expansion into a national body in 1937. Finally it traces its role after the Marco Polo Bridge Incident of July 1937 and its dissolution in 1938.

Wang's central claims concern the vanguard's dual character. Outwardly it presented itself as a non-partisan national salvation group, while in practice the Beiping Party committee ran a Party group inside it and Party members held leading posts. Wang cites 1936 directives from the Central Secretariat and Zhang Wentian urging the use of open or semi-open youth names, which the author says let the vanguard take over much of the function of the damaged Communist Youth League. The author also stresses its military and ideological training: drills in the Western Hills, summer camps, reading circles and periodicals. By Wang's figures, membership rose from about 300 to over 2,300 in Beiping by the end of 1936, and about 6,000 members nationally by February 1937. After the fall of Beiping and Tianjin, members joined guerrilla units and base areas, and registered numbers reached over 30,000 by April 1938.

Wang concludes that the vanguard preserved the gains of the December Ninth Movement in a more fixed organisational form and corrected the looseness of earlier student movements. Its members, in the author's phrase, moved from "taking up the pen" to "taking up the gun", forming a high-quality cadre corps that supplied the Party and the war behind enemy lines. The Central Committee decided in November 1938 to dissolve it in favour of local youth national salvation associations, as youth work shifted to the base areas. Read the original if you want a concise, Party-historiography account of how the Communist Party organised student youth in North China in 1935–38.
quoteEn: After the outbreak of the all-out War of Resistance, members who had been baptised in the December Ninth Movement went deep into the anti-Japanese base areas to wage armed struggle, truly making the transition in identity from "taking up the pen" to "taking up the gun".
quoteZh: 全民族抗战爆发之后，经过一二九运动洗礼的队员们深入各抗日根据地开展武装斗争，真正实现了从“拿笔”到“拿枪”的身份转变

glossary.explanation: A student-led anti-Japanese demonstration that began in Beiping on 9 December 1935, protesting Japanese pressure to detach North China. It is commemorated in Chinese historiography as a turning point in the national salvation movement.
A youth organisation founded in Beiping in February 1936 under Communist leadership, abbreviated Minxian dui. It posed as non-partisan and was dissolved in 1938.
A clash between Chinese and Japanese troops near Beiping on 7 July 1937, which marked the start of full-scale war.
The 1924–27 Nationalist–Communist alliance and Northern Expedition, which ended when the Nationalists turned on the Communists in 1927.

t: Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao in the early Republican Confucian religion debate: theoretical exploration and leadership role
zh: 陈独秀、李大钊在民初孔教论争中的理论探索及其领导作用
source: Science and Atheism (科学与无神论), 2025 no. 2
paras: This article revisits the debate over Confucianism as a state religion in the early Republic of China. After the 1911 Revolution, Kang Youwei, Chen Huanzhang and others petitioned parliament to make Confucianism the state religion and write it into the constitution. Gu and Hu argue that Chen Duxiu and Li Dazhao, as leaders of the New Culture Movement, took a leading part in opposing this. In the authors' account, they also began to examine theoretical questions about religion, which makes the episode an early point of contact between Marxism and the study of religion in China.

The article concentrates on the two state-religion campaigns of 1913–1914 and 1916–1917. It begins with the pre-debate period (1915–1916), when Chen and Li touched on religion in broader essays. It then covers Chen's rebuttal of Kang in New Youth (October 1916) and his exchange with the reader Yu Songhua. The remaining sections treat religion's essence and the nature of Confucianism, whether religion can be abolished, and the separation of religion and politics. A concluding section assesses the significance of the debate.

Gu and Hu argue that Chen judged religion by the standard of science and democracy. He held that religion is an otherworldly faith resting on divine command and imagination, whereas Confucianism is a worldly ethical system and so not a religion. He therefore called for science to replace religion and expected all religions to be abandoned. Li, by contrast, explained religion through economic life and social development. The authors see in his work elements of the materialist conception of history, especially after the October Revolution, and read the debate as a shift from Western scientific and democratic thought to Marxism. On politics, the authors report that Chen opposed writing Confucianism into the constitution on grounds of separation of religion and state and freedom of belief. He accepted a Confucian association only as a private body.

The authors conclude that the debate deepened the critique of religion and theism and advanced the New Culture Movement. They also see it as an initial union of Marxist views of religion with the study of Chinese religion, and as a first attempt at the Two Integrations in this field. They add that it left lessons for the Party's leadership of ideological debate: face problems directly, build theory, build a publishing platform such as New Youth, and guide young people. Read the original if you study the early Chinese Marxist view of religion, the New Culture Movement, or how contemporary scholars draw on this debate for ideological and political education.
quoteEn: Religion, as a thing, has as its fundamental spirit a faith that depends on another, taking divine will as the highest command; ethics and morality belong to self-reliant awakening, taking conscience as the highest command.
quoteZh: 宗教之为物……其根本精神，则属于依他的信仰，以神意为最高命令；伦理道德属于自依的觉悟，以良心为最高命令。

glossary.explanation: A formula in Chinese Party theory: integrating the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities (the first integration) and with China's fine traditional culture (the second). The article applies it retrospectively to early Marxist work on religion.
An intellectual movement from about 1915 that criticised Confucian tradition and promoted science and democracy. Its main journal was Chen Duxiu's New Youth.
The Marxist theory that material and economic conditions determine social and intellectual life. The article says Li Dazhao used it to analyse religion.
The principle that religious institutions and the state should be kept apart, which Chen used against making Confucianism the state religion.

t: A review of research on major foundational theoretical questions since the founding of the People's Republic
zh: 新中国成立以来重大基础理论问题研究述评
authors: Research Group on Major Foundational Theoretical and Practical Issues, Institute of Historical Theory
paras: This review, by a research group at the Institute of Historical Theory, surveys the major foundational theoretical questions that Chinese historians debated from 1949 to the present. It argues that these debates, though limited by their historical moment, answered the theoretical needs of the Party and people in revolution, construction and reform. In the authors' account, they enriched Chinese Marxist historiography and still offer intellectual resources for national rejuvenation.

The review covers six clusters of questions: the Marxist theory of social formations; the periodisation of ancient Chinese history; land-ownership systems; the sprouts of capitalism; the formation of the Han nation; and the evaluation of historical figures. It places most of them within the "five golden flowers" of the 1950s and 60s, tracing roots to the social-history debates of the 1920s and 30s. It follows each through early reform-era revival, later decline of attention, and renewed relevance. Related topics, such as the long continuity of Chinese feudal society and the Asiatic mode of production, are mentioned only briefly.

The authors treat the social-formation theory as the base of the others. Once the "five-stage" scheme was accepted, they argue, disputes arose over where slavery ended and feudalism began (the "three schools, five views"), what land system dominated feudal China, when capitalist sprouts appeared, and when the Han nation formed. They record the many competing positions, including single-line versus multi-line development and three-stage versus five-stage schemes. On historical figures, they endorse class analysis combined with historicism and concrete analysis. They say reform-era challenges to class analysis, under banners such as "multiple values", fed historical nihilism, which they describe as an attempt to undermine Party leadership.

The authors conclude that the debates delivered theoretical guidance for revolution and construction and many high-quality studies. In their view, the debates also created new subfields such as socio-economic history and ethnic history, and fostered a society-wide "theory fever" of open argument tied to practical needs. They call for a systematic review of this research to help build an autonomous Chinese knowledge system in history, and to support Chinese modernization and the work of forging a strong sense of community among the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a compact map of mid-century Chinese Marxist historiographical debates and how Party-aligned scholars now frame their legacy.)
quoteEn: Theoretical innovation has its basis in new great practice, and its precondition is academic reflection.
quoteZh: 理论创新的基础源于新的伟大实践，理论创新的前提在于学术反思。

glossary.explanation: A name for five major debates in 1950s–60s Chinese Marxist historiography: periodisation of ancient history, feudal land ownership, peasant wars, sprouts of capitalism, and formation of the Han nation.

The thesis that capitalist elements were emerging within late imperial Chinese society, notably Ming–Qing handicrafts, before Western intrusion. Mao Zedong's 1939 remark helped set the tone for the debate.
Stalin's summary of historical development as primitive, slave, feudal, capitalist and communist society, widely adopted in Chinese historiography after the 1930s.
In official Chinese discourse, a label for views seen as denying or distorting the Party's history and revolutionary legacy.
The official term for China's own path to modernization, promoted by the Party leadership and used here as a present-day framework for historical research.

glossary.zh: 铸牢中华民族共同体意识
glossary.en: forging a strong sense of community among the Chinese nation
glossary.literal: forge a firm consciousness of the Chinese national community
glossary.explanation: An official policy goal of strengthening shared national identity among China's ethnic groups.

t: Why China won the War of Resistance against Japan
st: Reading the "cave dialogue" between Mao Zedong and Edgar Snow
zh: 抗战为什么赢
zhSub: 读毛泽东与斯诺的“窑中对谈”
source: Journal of Studies of the War of Resistance against Japan (Kangri zhanzheng yanjiu), 2025 no. 1
paras: Discussions of Mao Zedong's contribution to strategy in the War of Resistance against Japan usually turn to On Protracted War (1938). Chen Hongmin looks instead at an earlier text: Mao's July 1936 conversations with the American journalist Edgar Snow in a Yan'an cave dwelling. Chen argues that Mao's prediction there, that China would win under three conditions, broadly matched the actual course of the war and explains why China prevailed.

The article first sets out the Mao–Snow exchange, drawing on the three related topics recorded in Selected Works of Mao Zedong and on Snow's Red Star over China. It then examines two of Mao's three conditions in turn: the formation of the Chinese anti-Japanese united front, and the formation of an international anti-Japanese united front. The third condition, revolutionary movements among the Japanese people and in Japan's colonies, receives only a brief assessment.

Chen stresses that Mao made his confident call, "Japan must lose, China must win", when only partial resistance was under way, the Nationalists and Communists were still at war and foreign support was negligible. In Chen's reading, the judgement rested on Mao's method of contradiction analysis, which treats internal causes as the basis of change and external causes as conditions. On this basis the national united front was the internal and principal condition, and the international front and Japanese revolution were external ones. Chen traces the national front from the Communists' calls after 1931, through the Xi'an Incident and the Marco Polo Bridge Incident (1937), to the Nationalist–Communist cooperation declared that September. He credits the front with mobilising ethnic minorities, overseas Chinese and relocated industry and universities, and says it fostered a consciousness of the Chinese nation as a community. For the international front, Chen follows Soviet aid, Western hesitation, the Pearl Harbor attack (1941), the creation of the China Theatre and the American volunteer air force (the "Flying Tigers").

Chen concludes that the Chinese and international fronts, the latter widened into the anti-fascist united front, were strong enough to defeat Japan, even though anti-war movements in Japan and its colonies never reached the level needed to halt the aggression. In Chen's view, history confirms the correctness of Mao's 1936 prediction. The article also cites Xi Jinping's statements on the people's war and on foreign assistance. Read the original if you study the historiography of the Anti-Japanese War, the Communist Party's united front theory, or how Chinese scholars present wartime Sino-American and international cooperation.
quoteEn: Mao Zedong's 1936 prediction that China would certainly win the War of Resistance under three conditions was basically consistent with the actual course of the full-scale war.
quoteZh: 毛泽东1936年关于中国在三个条件下一定能取得抗日战争胜利的预测，与全面抗战的实际进程基本一致。

glossary.explanation: The Communist-led policy of uniting all parties, classes and groups against Japanese aggression. It centred on Nationalist–Communist cooperation, formally established in September 1937.

Mao Zedong's philosophical method, set out in his essay On Contradiction (1937), which analyses things through their internal and external contradictions. The article treats it as the basis of his 1936 prediction.
Mao Zedong's May 1938 lecture predicting that the war against Japan would pass through three stages and end in Chinese victory. It is the text most often cited for his wartime strategic thought.

t: Japanese scholarship on the history of the Anti-Japanese National United Front: a review
st: Postwar studies from the late 1940s to the present
zh: 日本学界的抗日民族统一战线史研究回顾
source: Journal of Studies of Anti-Japanese War (Kangri zhanzheng yanjiu), 2025 no. 1
paras: This review surveys how Japanese scholars have studied the history of the Anti-Japanese National United Front since 1945. Ma argues that the research tracks developments in Japan's modern Chinese history field and shows changing Japanese perceptions of China. The article also asks what frameworks Japan relies on when discussing China, and what such research means for Japan today.

The article is organised in three periods. The first runs from the early postwar years to the 1960s, the second covers the 1970s to the 1990s, and the third covers the twenty-first century. It discusses a long list of Japanese historians, among them Nakanishi Tsutomu, Eto Shinkichi, Ishikawa Tadao, Nozawa Yutaka, Nishimura Shigeo, Tanaka Hitoshi, Hirano Tadashi, Mizuba Nobuo and Takahashi Nobuo. It ends with a concluding assessment of the trend as a whole.

In Ma's account, early postwar scholars treated the United Front as a revolutionary experience and a model for Japan's democratisation. They stressed the Chinese Communist Party's correctness and autonomy from the Comintern, and the 1960s anti-security-treaty struggle strengthened this concern. From the 1970s, doubts about a "revolution-centred view of history" and the rise of a "Republican-era view of history" moved attention elsewhere. Scholars turned to nationalism, democracy and state-building, to the Nationalist government, regional power-holders and intellectuals, and to mass movements beyond party relations. Since 2000 the topic has been folded into the study of contemporary China. Some work traces the origins of present-day political institutions, including "one country, two systems", to the United Front. Other work examines rural society and the Comintern's influence.

Ma concludes that Japanese interest has shifted from looking for a revolutionary model to understanding China's political and society, so that China moves from being a "subject" to being an "object" of study. Ma says the open challenges are how to understand contemporary China more accurately through history and how to use that study to rethink Japan's own problems. Ma also says Chinese scholars can use the survey to follow overseas research and deepen their own. Read the original if you want a detailed, name-by-name guide to postwar Japanese historiography of the United Front and the shifting frameworks behind it.
quoteEn: Behind this research trend lies the overall direction of Japanese studies of China: from searching for a revolutionary path that could serve as a reference for Japan to examining the dynamics of China's politics and society, an evolution that shows China shifting from "subject" to "object".
quoteZh: 这种研究态势的背后，反映出日本对华研究的整体趋势，从摸索可作为自身参考的革命方向，到洞察中国政治与社会的发展动态，其演变过程，呈现出将中国作为“主体”到作为“客体”的转变。

glossary.explanation: The policy of the Chinese Communist Party, adopted in the mid-1930s, of uniting parties, classes and groups, including the Nationalists, against Japanese aggression. Its main expression was the second Nationalist–Communist cooperation from 1937.
An approach that equates modern Chinese history with the history of the revolution and of the Chinese Communist Party. The article says Japanese scholars began to question it in the 1970s.

An approach that treats the Republic of China period (1911–1949) as an era of modern nation-state building and stresses empirical research. The article says it influenced Japanese scholarship in the 1980s and 1990s.
The policy under which Hong Kong, Macao and, in intention, Taiwan keep their own systems within China. Some Japanese scholars cited in the article link it historically to the United Front.

t: On the programme for transforming Chinese society in "The Great Union of the Popular Masses"
zh: 论《民众的大联合》改造中国社会的方案
source: Mao Zedong Thought Studies (Mao Zedong Sixiang Yanjiu), 2025 no. 1
paras: This article rereads "The Great Union of the Popular Masses", which the young Mao Zedong wrote in 1919 for the Xiang River Review. It asks what programme for remaking China the essay set out, and what it shows about the thinking of young intellectuals at the time. Chen and Yang argue that the essay proposed a reformist route to transformation, shaped by the October Revolution and the May Fourth Movement. In their reading, it also reflects Mao's own path before he became a Marxist.

The article first examines why the essay was written. It points to warlord fragmentation and the misrule of Zhang Jingyao in Hunan, and to the impact of the October Revolution and the May Fourth Movement. It then sets out the essay's content under three headings: why China had to be transformed, which force could do it, and by what method. A final section reads the text as showing Mao's sense of historical responsibility and his contradictory state of mind.

On necessity, Chen and Yang say Mao concluded that the union of the powerful, the aristocrats and the capitalists had pushed the country to an extreme, so thorough change was needed. On the force to rely on, they say Mao held that popular unions are historically inevitable and have practical grounds. Groups with shared interests form small unions, and these join into a great union that can match the unions of the powerful. The method is the "revolution of the voice", which has three strands: the voice of bread, of freedom and of equality. In the authors' account, bread is the precondition of the other two, and the other two secure it.

The authors argue that the essay shows Mao's ambition to save the nation, but also his attraction to anarchism. They cite his preference for provincial self-determination and a mild course over violent revolution, since force used against force would only bring more force. The authors note that this view was shared by many progressive intellectuals of the time. In their conclusion, the proposals did not meet their aims in practice but were valuable training, and they hastened Mao's choice of Marxism-Leninism. Read the original if you study Mao's early thought, the intellectual transition from reformism and anarchism to Marxism, or how Chinese scholarship now frames this text.
quoteEn: The great union of the popular masses was the only way out, and the fundamental force to rely on, for transforming Chinese society.
quoteZh: 民众大联合是改造中国社会的唯一出路与根本依靠力量。

t: The New Hunan Daily's organisation of the "Li Sixi thought" discussion
zh: 《新湖南报》组织“李四喜思想”讨论研究
paras: Han Xiaoqing examines a propaganda campaign run by the New Hunan Daily, the Hunan provincial Party organ, between July 1951 and January 1952. The paper invented a fictional village cadre, Li Sixi, who stopped working for the revolution once land reform had given him land, a wife, a child and Youth League membership. Han argues that the discussion was a successful case of Party propaganda and ideological guidance. In Han's account, it overcame complacency among rural cadres after land reform and was then promoted nationwide by the Central Committee. Han notes that existing scholarship mostly treats it as peasant education, and instead reads it as propaganda and thought work.

The article has four parts. It first sets out the background and the occasion: cadre slackness after the 1950 Land Reform Law, the first national propaganda work conference of 1951, and the experience of the editor Zhang Yulin, whose fieldwork in Changsha county produced the prototype, the cadre Zhu Zhongli. It then analyses three methods of steering the discussion. A third part assesses results in Hunan and elsewhere, including the Central Committee's circular of 19 September 1951 and coverage in the People's Daily. A short conclusion draws lessons for present propaganda work.

Han's central argument is that the paper kept control of a discussion open to readers with differing views. First, it published summary articles after one month, two months and five months, assessing progress and setting the next direction. Second, it printed dissenting letters, for example that cadres should rotate in office or that their pay should rise, alongside many rebuttals. Han argues that readers thereby reached the intended conclusion unprompted. Third, it ran testimony from Zhu Zhongli himself, revealed as the prototype only on 7 January 1952, so readers could see that holding such views was not fatal. Han adds that the final review called for combining ideological education with solving cadres' practical difficulties.

Han concludes that the campaign succeeded because it chose a real and widespread problem, was carefully organised, and received backing from the Party centre and national media. The article cites over 2,300 submissions and similar campaigns in other provinces, including a "Wang Xiuzhen thought" discussion among Tianjin workers. Han suggests that, in a period of great change and the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, this experience still offers lessons for ideological work and public-opinion guidance. Read the original if you study early People's Republic propaganda methods, Party press practice or the history of rural cadre education, and want the detailed documentary record.
quoteEn: The "Li Sixi thought" discussion launched by the New Hunan Daily was a successful case of the CPC, in the early years of the People's Republic, using propaganda work to educate rural cadres and guide trends of thought.
quoteZh: 《新湖南报》发起的“李四喜思想”讨论，是新中国成立初期中共通过宣传工作教育乡村干部，引导思想动向的成功案例。

glossary.explanation: The redistribution of landlords' land to poor peasants carried out by the Communist Party, in newly liberated areas under the 1950 Land Reform Law. It was largely completed by around 1952.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: A central goal in Party discourse, especially since Xi Jinping, of restoring China's national strength and international standing.
A newspaper run by a Party committee at a given level that serves as its official voice, such as the New Hunan Daily for the Hunan provincial committee.

t: Hadapu and related questions on the Red Army's Long March
zh: 哈达铺与红军长征相关问题研究
paras: Mao Lihong examines what happened at Hadapu (in present-day Gansu) when the Central Red Army reached it on 18 September 1935, and why it mattered for the Long March. On 22 September Mao Zedong told a meeting of regimental-level and higher cadres that the army must complete the original plan of going north to resist Japan, and "first of all go to northern Shaanxi". The article argues that, although there is already considerable scholarship, several details need clarifying, and that Hadapu was a pivotal link in the Party's decision to settle in northern Shaanxi.

The article is organised in four parts. It first sorts the competing accounts of the newspapers read at Hadapu. It then considers Hadapu as a "refuelling station" for the Red Army. Next it relates the Hadapu meeting to the Eljie (Eqiu/Eryu) and Bangluozhen meetings. It ends with the strategic significance of fixing the destination. Sources include memoirs by Ye Jianying, Li Weihan, Yang Chengwu, Geng Biao, Liu Ying and Nie Rongzhen, Zhang Wentian's reading notes, and chronologies and Party histories.

On newspapers, Mao Lihong finds that sources variously name Tianjin's Ta Kung Pao, the Shanxi Daily and other Kuomintang papers. The author concludes only that learning from newspapers is widely accepted, and that so large a decision could not rest on press reports alone. Jia Tuofu's briefing at Bangluozhen supplied further intelligence, and the "newspapers decide direction" story reflects the army's longing for a stable base. On the meetings, Mao Lihong holds that Eljie set out the idea, Hadapu clarified the direction and Bangluozhen made the formal decision, so Hadapu was the hinge. As a "refuelling station" it gave supplies, medical care, recruits, reorganisation into the Shaanxi–Gansu Detachment, and morale, helped by the army's discipline and ethnic policy. It was also the only such station visited by all three front armies.

Mao Lihong concludes that settling in northern Shaanxi advanced the Long March's success. It also kept to the northward anti-Japanese line and helped shift the revolution's centre of gravity from south to north. The author presents Hadapu as an important choice that carried the Chinese revolution through its lowest point and toward a major turning point. Read the original if you want a source-based account of the Hadapu newspaper accounts and of the Eljie–Hadapu–Bangluozhen sequence in Chinese Party history writing.
quoteEn: Therefore, as regards settling in northern Shaanxi, the Eljie meeting put forward the idea, the Hadapu meeting clarified the direction, and the Bangluozhen meeting made the decision.
quoteZh: 因此，就落脚陕北而言，俄界会议是提出构想，哈达铺会议是明确方向，榜罗镇会议是作出决策。

glossary.explanation: The Red Army's strategic retreat of 1934–36 from the southern base areas to the northwest. It is a central episode in the Chinese Communist Party's official history.
The name given to the reorganised northward-marching force of the First Front Army after the Eljie meeting. Its formal establishment was announced at Hadapu on 22 September 1935.

t: The construction of an aesthetic community in Yan'an theatre production
zh: 论延安戏剧生产的审美共同体建构
paras: How did theatre workers and ordinary people in the Yan'an period come to form a shared aesthetic world? Yang Funing and Li Youjun argue that Yan'an theatre production built a new "aesthetic community" (shenmei gongtongti). Its ideals were national liberation and equality for all, its goal was the unity of politics and aesthetics, and its main route was mass participation in artistic production. The authors present this as a new model that tied intellectuals to workers, peasants and soldiers.

The article is a historical-aesthetic study of theatre in the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region, roughly 1938 to 1947. It is organised in four parts: aesthetic equality as the foundation, then a community of emotion, a community of national destiny, and a community of education. The cases include the new opera The White-Haired Girl, the yangge play Brother and Sister Reclaim the Wasteland, Qin opera plays such as Blood and Tears Hatred, the Mei-hu play Everyone Is Happy, and the folk artist Li Bu in the Shaan-Gan-Ning People's Theatre Troupe. The authors draw on Mao Zedong's Yan'an Talks, press reports, letters and a 2022 interview.

The authors first argue that early Yan'an theatre was hampered by an unequal relationship between elite culture and folk culture. Intellectuals overrode popular taste, and the 1940–41 vogue for "big plays" showed this. Equality emerged after the 1942 Talks, through the new yangge movement, the reform of old drama and collective creation. On that basis, the authors say, shared feeling developed: creators empathised with peasants' suffering, and audiences responded with criticism and revisions that fed back into the plays. National destiny was then articulated through characters such as Wang Renhou, who encouraged audiences to see their own fate in a common struggle. Education worked through plays that reformed idlers (erliuzi), and through intellectuals learning from folk artists as well as teaching them.

The authors conclude that the Yan'an aesthetic community was successful and made a major contribution to resistance to Japan and class liberation, and that classics such as The White-Haired Girl remain vital. They hold that equal aesthetic relations are what separates socialist art from earlier art. Citing Xi Jinping's 2014 speech on literature and art, they say contemporary theatre, challenged by digital media, should again write about the people's shared destiny, feelings and ideals. They add that this experience could offer a literary-theoretical interpretation of a community with a shared future for mankind. Read the original if you are interested in Yan'an cultural history, the Party's mass-line approach to the arts, or how Chinese scholars link that heritage to current cultural policy.
quoteEn: The establishment of equal aesthetic relations is also shown in the continual enrichment and adjustment of theatrical forms.
quoteZh: 审美平等关系的建立还表现在戏剧形式的不断丰富和调整中。

glossary.explanation: A group of people bound together by shared aesthetic experience, here created through theatre. The authors use it to describe the bond between theatre workers and the masses in Yan'an.

glossary.literal: Talks at the Yan'an Forum on Literature and Art
glossary.explanation: Mao Zedong's 1942 speeches at the Yan'an Forum on Literature and Art. They set the Party line that art should serve workers, peasants and soldiers, and be integrated with them.
A short song-and-dance drama developed from northern Shaanxi folk yangge. It was reworked in Yan'an in the early 1940s as a popular vehicle for new political content.
A term in Border Region campaigns for loafers and gamblers regarded as shirking labour. Cultural work was meant to reform them into productive peasants.

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Official concept of Xi Jinping, used in foreign policy and theory to describe a vision of global interdependence and shared development.

t: The emergence, interaction and transformation of the concept of "modernization" in the New Democratic Revolution period
zh: 新民主主义革命时期“现代化”概念的出场、互动与嬗变
source: Journal of the Party School of the CPC Central Committee (National Academy of Governance), 2025 no. 1
paras: Xu Cenchen takes up a question about the intellectual history of modernization in China. A common view holds that the Communist Party's modernization thinking began with Mao Zedong's post-1949 formula of a socialist country with modern industry, agriculture, science and culture. Xu argues that debate on the concept was already lively in the New Democratic Revolution period (roughly 1919–1949). The article contends that the concept emerged from earlier discussions of "modern civilization", fused with the idea of national rejuvenation, and was reinterpreted by Communists and left-wing intellectuals from a historical-materialist standpoint.

The article is organised chronologically and thematically in three parts. The first traces the concept's appearance in the 1920s and its spread in 1930s journals, including the 1933 special issue of Shenbao Monthly on China's modernization. The second examines how "modernization" and "national rejuvenation" (minzu fuxing) converged after 1931, with debates centred on culture and the countryside. The third turns to Communist figures and left-wing writers such as Qu Qiubai, Ai Siqi, Yang Xingzhi, Mao Zedong, Zhou Enlai and Dong Biwu.

Xu's central claim is that the two concepts complemented each other. According to Xu, national rejuvenation gave modernization a national perspective and helped dispel its identification with "Westernization", as thinkers such as Zhang Xiruo, Chen Gaoyong and Feng Youlan distinguished the two. In turn, modernization gave the emotionally charged call for rejuvenation a more analytical framework covering culture, economy and science. Xu then argues that Communists differed from other intellectuals in three ways. They treated revolution against imperialism and feudal forces as the precondition of modernization, drawing on Mao's "On Contradiction". They used the concept sparingly, mainly for military and technical matters, owing to their constrained political position. And from 1944–45 onwards they placed industrialization first, a line that Xu traces through Mao's "On Coalition Government", the Second Plenum of the 7th Central Committee (1949) and the Common Programme.

Xu concludes that the debates freed Chinese thought from the narrow East–West cultural contest and gave it a world-historical view. Xu holds that the Party's combination of Marxist theory with Chinese revolutionary and construction practice, and its choice of industrialization as the starting point, localised the concept in China and prepared later formulations such as "socialist industrialization" and the "four modernizations". Read the original if you study the conceptual history of modernization in modern China, or want the Chinese scholarly case for tracing Party thinking on modernization back before 1949.
quoteEn: "Modernization" gave "national rejuvenation" a more theoretical analytical perspective, prompting Chinese people to examine the basic path of national rejuvenation scientifically from the angles of cultural construction, economic development, science and technology.
quoteZh: “现代化”为“民族复兴”提供了更为学理性的分析视角，促使国人从文化建设、经济发展、科学技术等诸多角度科学审视民族复兴的基本路径。

glossary.explanation: Mao Zedong's term for the stage of the Chinese revolution from 1919 to 1949, led by the proletariat and aimed at overthrowing imperialism, feudalism and bureaucrat-capitalism before the transition to socialism.
A slogan widely used in 1930s China in response to the Japanese threat and national crisis. It was later taken up in the Party's concept of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.
The view or process of adopting Western culture and institutions. In 1920s–30s debates, "wholesale Westernization" was an influential and contested position.
The post-1949 goal of modernizing agriculture, industry, national defence and science and technology. It was prominently revived by Zhou Enlai and Deng Xiaoping in the late 1970s.

t: Big economic provinces shouldering the main burden: setting an example in promoting common prosperity for all the people
zh: 经济大省挑大梁，要在促进全体人民共同富裕上“作示范”
paras: This commentary, published in New Xiangjiang Review in 2025, takes up Xi Jinping's instruction at the Jiangsu delegation to the National People's Congress on 5 March 2025 that big economic provinces must 'shoulder the main burden' (挑大梁) to achieve the goals of the 14th Five-Year Plan. Gong and Zhu argue that these provinces are pivotal to national development and must contribute more to high-quality development and the overall national picture.

The authors first set out the national strategic significance of the requirement, tracing Xi's repeated statements since July 2022. They then turn to its practical paths, following the four points Xi gave to Jiangsu: take the lead in integrating scientific and industrial innovation, strive to be first in deeper reform and higher-level opening up, move ahead in implementing major national strategies, and set an example in promoting common prosperity.

On significance, the authors invoke the Marxist dialectic of part and whole: the big provinces are the 'ballast' of the national economy and an 'engine' for surrounding regions. They cite figures that these provinces hold under a fifth of the national territory, over half the population and more than 60 per cent of GDP, and that Guangdong and Jiangsu each approached 14 trillion yuan in 2024. On common prosperity, they recall Deng Xiaoping's idea of some regions getting rich first and leading others. Given uneven regional, urban–rural and income development, they say the big provinces should help less developed areas, advance rural revitalisation, reform income distribution and equalise public services.

On practice, the authors call for more research investment, firms as the main innovators, market-oriented factor reform, equal treatment of all ownership types and a better business environment. They also want provinces to link up with strategies such as Yangtze River Delta integration and the Greater Bay Area, with a 'national chessboard' mindset. For common prosperity they propose industrial transfer, paired assistance, vocational training bases in central and western regions, and replicable models, citing Zhejiang's demonstration zone for common prosperity. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary translates Xi's 2025 instructions on regional leadership and common prosperity into tasks for individual provinces.
quoteEn: Big economic provinces are developing faster and have the foundation to achieve common prosperity first; they should explore actively in promoting common prosperity for all the people and play a demonstrating and leading role.
quoteZh: 经济大省发展较快，具备率先实现共同富裕的基础，应在促进全体人民共同富裕上积极探索，发挥示范带动作用

glossary.explanation: A goal of shared wealth that Chinese leaders describe as an essential requirement of socialism. It has been given renewed emphasis under Xi Jinping, including through the Zhejiang demonstration zone.

glossary.literal: big economic provinces carry the main beam
glossary.explanation: A phrase used by Xi Jinping from 2022 onward, calling on the wealthiest provinces to take the lead in stabilising and driving the national economy.
The official economic goal that stresses innovation, efficiency and sustainability over raw growth rates, prominent since the 19th Party Congress (2017).
A national strategy launched in 2017 to develop agriculture, villages and rural incomes, and to narrow the urban–rural gap.

t: Layers and truth-seeking: an examination of how Mao Zedong's status at the Zunyi Conference has been written in history
zh: 层累与求真：关于遵义会议毛泽东地位历史书写的考察
source: Research on the Soviet Areas (Suqu yanjiu), 2025 no. 1
paras: Did the Zunyi Conference of 1935 establish Mao Zedong's leadership of the Party and the Red Army? The authors treat this as the most contested question about the conference. They take it up from the angle of academic history and social-cultural history, tracing how mainland official and scholarly accounts have described Mao's status since 1949. They argue that official wording was built up in layers and was in turn shaped by scholars' truth-seeking research, and that the two have usefully influenced each other.

The article has two main parts. The first follows the official narrative through the Party's three historical resolutions (1945, 1981, 2021), speeches by Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping, and Party-history works from Liao Gailong and Hu Qiaomu in the 1950s to the 2021 Short History of the Communist Party of China. The second follows scholarship: textbooks by Hu Hua, He Ganzhi and Li Xin up to 1978, then the mainstream and dissenting views after reform and opening up.

On the official side, the authors identify a steady accumulation of formulations. "Established" replaces the 1945 "began". The leadership's scope is specified as the Party and the Red Army. Deng Xiaoping's 1965 concept of a "core" is added, then Mao's correct line, and finally, under Hu and Xi, the qualifier "Marxist". The 2021 resolution largely reproduces Xi's 2016 wording and restores the phrase "in fact", which Deng had had cut from a draft of the 1981 resolution. The authors read this as a response to scholarly debate. On the scholarly side, most writers followed the official line. Since the 1980s, seven dissenting positions have appeared, including that Mao was one member of a collective led by Zhang Wentian, and that his position was secured only after the Goubadi meeting, in August or November 1935, in 1943 or at the Seventh Congress (1945). The authors say these supplement the traditional view rather than reject it.

The authors conclude that official narrative has strongly standardised scholarship without replacing it, and that absorbing research findings has made the 2021 formulation more precise. They reject the idea that Party-history research should never go beyond the resolutions. They call on officials to separate research from propaganda and to uphold the principle of "no forbidden zones in academic research". They also ask Party-history scholars for self-discipline: original work, no duplicate publication, and no adulatory language. Read the original if you study the historiography of the Zunyi Conference or want a detailed comparison of official wordings on Mao's status over seven decades.
quoteEn: Since reform and opening up, the changes in how Mao Zedong's status at the Zunyi Conference has been written are a typical footnote to the academicisation of Party-history research.
quoteZh: 改革开放以来，关于遵义会议毛泽东地位历史书写的变化，正是中共党史研究学术化发展的一个典型脚注。

glossary.explanation: An enlarged Politburo meeting held in January 1935 in Zunyi, Guizhou, during the Long March. Party histories treat it as a turning point in the Party's military and political leadership.
Three authoritative Central Committee resolutions (1945, 1981, 2021) that set the Party's official assessment of its history.
The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched in 1978. Here it marks the period of a freer research environment.

glossary.en: no forbidden zones in academic research
glossary.literal: academic research has no forbidden zones
glossary.explanation: A slogan from the reform era that research topics should not be placed off limits. The authors invoke it to defend open scholarly debate in Party history.

t: The inner mechanism by which the guiding ideology of the Communist Party of China leads self-reform and social revolution
zh: 中国共产党指导思想引领自我革命和社会革命的内在机理
source: Journal of China Jinggangshan Cadre Institute, 2025 no. 1
paras: Zhang Guoyu asks how the guiding ideology of the Communist Party of China generates lasting attraction and leadership over Party members, cadres and the people. Starting from the 20th Party Congress (2022) claim that Marxism, adapted to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, explains the Party's success, the author argues that existing studies concentrate on the objects and methods of ideological leadership. Zhang instead looks at how the ideology produces influence from within. The thesis is that three core elements of Marxism account for this force, both in the Party's self-reform and in leading social revolution.

The article has five parts. It first identifies the three cores of the Party's guiding ideology: the inevitability of communism and the mission of each person's free and all-round development, a political standpoint of serving the great majority, and a scientific worldview and methodology. It then traces how Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development and Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era have each kept and renewed these cores. Two parts then explain the mechanism for self-reform and for social revolution, and a short conclusion follows.

Zhang's central move is to treat the Party as an organisation answering three questions: why it exists, what it ultimately aims at, and how it builds its capacity. These correspond to relations of space (organisation and society), time (short-term tasks and long-term mission) and self (intention and ability). In the author's account, the Party's founding idea, its communist mission and its scientific methodology answer these questions and so drive the Party's self-reform. Because the Party claims no interests apart from the people's, Zhang argues, it can correct errors and win voluntary support. Zhang adds that the three cores operate along relational, task and pathway dimensions, none of which can be dropped. The author contrasts this with firms, governments and bourgeois parties, which the article says rest on contract, coercion or the exchange of votes for benefits. Zhang describes a reversed leadership relation in which the Party serves the people while raising their consciousness.

Zhang concludes that the Party must keep building itself ideologically and theoretically, and must use self-reform to drive social revolution and move towards the 'final goal' of communism. Solving the problems unique to a large party, the author says, requires clear and firm adherence to its guiding ideology. The article gives a normative, organisation-theory account of Party ideology as an internal source of authority. Read the original if you want to see how a Party School scholar frames ideological leadership as a link between Party-building and mass leadership, or if you study official Chinese theorising on the Party's guiding ideology.
quoteEn: The influence, leadership and guiding power of an ideology are fundamentally generated from within the ideology itself, outward, and are determined by its own essential attributes.
quoteZh: 一种思想的影响力、领导力、引领力，从根本来说是思想自身由内而外生成的，是思想自身的本质属性决定的。

glossary.explanation: Official term for the Party's efforts to discipline, purify and renew itself. It is a central theme of Party-building discourse under Xi Jinping.
A concept first put forward in Xi Jinping's report to the 19th Party Congress (2017). It refers to the non-coercive influence of the Party's ideas on cadres and the public.

t: The Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region Council: a successful exploration of building a New Democratic regime
zh: 陕甘宁边区参议会：新民主主义政权建设的成功探索
paras: This short commentary, published in Study Times in March 2025, asks what the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region Council (canshenghui) contributed to building a New Democratic regime during the War of Resistance against Japan. Zhang and Liu argue that it was the earliest, most fully developed and most typical democratic institution in the anti-Japanese base areas, and that it was a model for other bases.

The article draws on four council sessions held between 1939 and 1946. It first describes the basic framework of the regime that the council explored, then its effects on governance in the border region, and finally four lessons drawn from the experience.

On structure, the authors point to a three-tier system of border-region, county and township councils, and to the 1946 Principles of the Constitution of the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region. They also stress the "three-thirds system", under which Communists, non-Party left-progressives and centrists each held one third of seats, and they cite the 1941 session's 219 delegates and more than 380 proposals. In Zhang and Liu's account, the council united social strata, including enlightened gentry and ethnic minority figures. It improved decision-making, for example through Li Dingming's proposal for "crack troops and simple administration". It also laid a foundation for the people's congress system and for the system of multiparty cooperation and political consultation led by the Communist Party.

The authors list four lessons: upholding Party leadership, ensuring the people are masters of the country, maintaining criticism and self-criticism, and seeking truth from facts. They present these as historical experience for whole-process people's democracy. Read the original if you want a concise, official-style account of how the Party presents its wartime base-area councils as precursors of present-day political institutions.
quoteEn: The leadership of the proletarian party is always the most essential feature and the most fundamental guarantee of people's democracy.
quoteZh: 无产阶级政党的领导，始终是人民民主最本质的特征和最根本的保证。

glossary.explanation: A principle for anti-Japanese base-area governments proposed in 1940. It allotted one third of seats each to Communists, non-Party left-progressives and centrists, to broaden the united front.
A concept in current Party discourse that describes China's democracy as covering every stage of political life, not only elections.
Mao Zedong's theory of a transitional revolutionary stage in China, led by the proletariat in a coalition of several classes, before socialism.
The representative assembly of the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region, elected at border-region, county and township levels, with legislative and oversight powers.

t: A historical examination of the Shenzhen Special Zone currency in the early reform and opening-up period
zh: 改革开放初期深圳特区货币的历史考察
source: Studies on Party History (Zhonggong dangshi yanjiu), 2024 no. 5
paras: Between 1979 and 1985 the central government planned to issue a freely convertible local currency in the Shenzhen Special Economic Zone, but in the end decided not to. Xiao Anmiao notes that existing studies of this "special zone currency" mostly stress the effects of opening to the outside world. The article instead reads the episode as a case of central–local relations. Xiao argues that the plan was dropped because it could not be reconciled with managing the relationship between the zone and the rest of the planned economy, and with the shift of reform from the local to the national level.

Drawing on leaders' speeches, State Council and People's Bank of China documents, and local statistics, the article follows the plan through three rounds of deliberation. The first began in 1979, when Guangdong raised the issue, and ended in suspension in 1982. The second was driven by the Hong Kong negotiations from 1982 to 1983. The third began in 1984 around Deng Xiaoping's inspection tour and ended with rejection in 1985. Before these, the article sketches the pressures of the planned economy, the dual-track price system and the Bretton Woods background.

Xiao's central claim is that the currency question followed from the policy of "relaxing the first line and controlling the second line". Freer use of Hong Kong dollars in Shenzhen brought a "three-currency" situation of renminbi, foreign exchange certificates and Hong Kong dollars. According to the author's data, the renminbi's share of circulation fell sharply, and reverse flows of goods and certificates into the interior drew criticism in 1982. Central figures such as Chen Yun feared that the second line could not be held and that the zone would harm the non-special-zone economy. Others, including Deng Xiaoping, worried about the impact on the renminbi, but also saw a currency as needed to attract foreign capital and to prepare for Hong Kong's return. Xiao treats the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress's 1985 rejection, on the ground that "one country should not have two currencies", as the point where the argument settled.

Xiao concludes that China then had three kinds of economic region (planned, experimental, highly marketised), with Shenzhen as the pivot between them. As reform spread from points to the whole country, local currency reform became comprehensive currency reform, and the special zone currency was abandoned. The author warns against treating reform and opening up as a simple linear process, since this case shows its complexity. Read the original if you are interested in the history of Shenzhen, monetary policy and the Party's internal decision-making during reform and opening up, or in a documented case of central–local bargaining.
quoteEn: How to handle the relationship between the centre and the localities properly was both the key to advancing reform and opening up and the key to whether the central authorities would agree to issue a special zone currency.
quoteZh: 如何妥善处理中央与地方的关系，既是推动改革开放的关键，也是中央是否同意发行特区货币的关键。

glossary.explanation: The policy line launched in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping, moving China from a highly centralised planned economy towards market mechanisms and engagement with the world economy.
Areas such as Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Shantou and Xiamen given special policies from 1979–80 to attract foreign investment and test market-oriented measures. They were first called "export special zones".
A proposed locally issued, freely convertible currency for Shenzhen. It was designed and sample notes were printed, but it was never issued.

glossary.en: relaxing the first line and controlling the second line
glossary.literal: loosen the first line, control the second line
glossary.explanation: The principle of freer movement across the border between the zone and Hong Kong (the first line), with strict controls on the boundary between the zone and the mainland interior (the second line).
A certificate issued by the Bank of China from April 1980 for foreigners and overseas Chinese to use in place of foreign currency within China.

t: Carrying forward the spirit of the Zunyi Conference and continuing to adapt Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
zh: 弘扬遵义会议精神 不断推进马克思主义中国化时代化
paras: Xin Xiangyang takes the Zunyi Conference of January 1935, held during the Long March, as a turning point in the Party's history. The article asks what lessons its spirit offers for adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Xin argues that the conference's experience points to five requirements: a strong leadership core, the Two Integrations, seeking truth from facts, independence and self-reliance, and Party unity.

This is a commentary in a Party theory journal, framed by Xi Jinping's 2015 and 2021 remarks at Zunyi and in Guizhou. Xin first recounts the background: the failure of the fifth encirclement campaign under the "Left" dogmatist line, the fall in Central Red Army strength from over 86,000 to just over 30,000, and the formation of a new three-person military group in March 1935. Each of the five sections then pairs a historical episode with quotations from Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping, Xi Jinping and Party resolutions, and ends with a task for the new era.

Xin's central claim is that the conference dealt with more than military and organisational errors. In this account it settled the question of independence and self-reliance: whether the Chinese revolution would follow the Comintern and dogmatism or find its own path under Marxism-Leninism. Xin presents the Zunyi leaders' open and inclusive conduct as evidence of both Marxist truth and the wisdom of fine traditional Chinese culture, and describes the meeting's broad participation and criticism and self-criticism as a model of democratic centralism. Xin also treats the conference as the start of Mao's leadership of the first-generation central leadership, and links this to the present by calling Xi Jinping the main founder of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and by invoking the Two Establishes.

Xin concludes that, on the new journey, Party members should study Xi's directives, uphold the Two Establishes and the Two Upholds, and continue the Two Integrations. They should also address China's own problems from its national conditions, and maintain unity around the Central Committee with Xi at its core, so as to advance Chinese modernization. Read the original if you want to see how a leading Party theorist presents the Zunyi Conference as a source of current doctrine on leadership, theoretical innovation and Party discipline.
quoteEn: Although the Zunyi Conference directly resolved military and organisational problems, more importantly it fundamentally resolved the question of independence and self-reliance.
quoteZh: 遵义会议虽然直接解决的是军事问题和组织问题，但更重要的是从根本上解决独立自主的问题

glossary.explanation: The principle of combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. The second element was added in official discourse under Xi Jinping.
A formula from the Party's 2021 historical resolution. It affirms Xi Jinping's position as core of the Central Committee and the Party as a whole, and the guiding role of his thought.
The Party's call to uphold Xi Jinping's core position in the Central Committee and the Party, and to uphold the authority and centralised, unified leadership of the Central Committee.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party constitution in 2017.
The official term for China's path of modernization, as defined by the Party since the 20th Party Congress (2022).
A principle associated with Mao Zedong's 1930s writings and later Deng Xiaoping. It calls for policy based on investigation of actual conditions rather than doctrine.

t: The Zunyi Conference: turning a new page
zh: 遵义会议：翻开了新的一页
paras: This short historical commentary, published in the Party journal Dangjian in 2025, revisits the Zunyi Conference of 15–17 January 1935. Yang Mingwei argues that the meeting was a life-and-death turning point in Party history. In Yang's account, it in effect established Mao Zedong's leadership in the Party Central Committee and the Red Army, began the formation of a first-generation central leadership collective with Mao at its core, and opened a new stage in which the Party solved China's revolutionary problems independently.

The article follows events in three stages. It first traces the run-up: the heavy losses at the Xiang River at the end of 1934, the dispute over where the Central Red Army should go, and the successive meetings at Tongdao, Liping and Houchang, ending with the capture of Zunyi on 7 January 1935. It then describes the conference itself and Mao's role in it. Finally it follows the weeks after the conference, including the battle at Tucheng, the Four Crossings of the Chishui River, and the Gougba meeting.

Yang's central argument is that the conference's substance was a verdict on the military line. Mao criticised Bo Gu's explanation that enemy strength caused the defeat of the fifth anti-encirclement campaign, and attributed it to errors in command, strategy and tactics. In Yang's account, Bo Gu and Otto Braun (Li De) had replaced mobile warfare with positional and blockhouse warfare. The meeting, according to the article, added Mao to the Politburo Standing Committee, abolished the "three-person group" and stripped Bo Gu and Li De of supreme military command. Yang adds that Zhang Wentian then took over general responsibility from Bo Gu, with Mao's agreement, and that a new three-man military group of Zhou Enlai, Mao and Wang Jiaxiang was formed after Gougba.

Yang concludes that Zunyi ended the rule of Wang Ming's "Left" adventurism in the Central Committee. The article credits it with saving the Party, the Red Army and the revolution, and with laying the foundation for completing the Long March. After it, Yang writes, the Party began to apply the basic principles of Marxism-Leninism independently and became politically mature. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed narrative of the Zunyi Conference and the weeks around it, as presented in a Party publication.
quoteEn: After the Zunyi Conference, the Communist Party of China began to apply the basic principles of Marxism-Leninism independently to the major questions deciding the fate of the Chinese revolution, and began to mature politically.
quoteZh: 自遵义会议后，中国共产党开始独立自主地运用马克思列宁主义的基本原理，解决中国革命前途命运的重大问题，在政治上开始走向成熟。

glossary.explanation: An enlarged Politburo meeting held in Zunyi, Guizhou, on 15–17 January 1935 during the Long March. Official Party history treats it as the point at which Mao Zedong became the effective leader of the Party and the Red Army.
The strategic retreat of the Red Army from its Jiangxi base from late 1934, ending in north-west China in 1935–36. It is a foundational episode in the Party's official history.

The official Party label for the ultra-radical political and military line that dominated the Central Committee in the early 1930s. Party histories associate it with Wang Ming and, in military matters, with Bo Gu and Otto Braun.
The Red Army's campaigns against the Nationalist government's repeated military "encirclement and suppression" drives on the Communist base areas. The fifth campaign (1933–34) ended in defeat.

t: Mao Zedong's strategic thinking in responding to the "anti-China chorus"
zh: 毛泽东应对“反华大合唱”的战略思想
source: Mao Zedong Deng Xiaoping Theory Studies, 2024 no. 10
paras: This article asks how Mao Zedong dealt with what he called the "anti-China chorus", the wave of external hostility that confronted the new People's Republic in the Cold War, and what that experience offers today. Hu Tianjiao argues that Mao distinguished between hostile forces of different kinds, assessed their overall character from a global perspective, and held that negative factors could turn into positive ones. In Hu's account, Mao saw the fundamental answer in unity and in independent, self-reliant socialist construction.
