zh: 毛泽东诗词中的英雄形象
paras: Wang Jianxin, in a commentary first published in Study Times (Xuexi Shibao) on 23 September 2022, asks how heroes and heroism are portrayed in Mao Zedong's poems and lyrics. The author argues that the heroic spirit is the enduring thread running through Mao's verse. It rests on a deep ideological content, and Mao combined an intense admiration for heroes with a firm rejection of the 'heroes make history' view.

The article opens with Mao's boyhood reading in 1910 of a collection of biographies of world heroes, which, Wang says, made him see China's need for strong figures. It then proceeds in thematic sections: Mao's own youthful heroic self-image and sense of mission; his judgements on figures of the past, from the Yellow Emperor and Qu Yuan to Jia Yi, Cao Cao, Zu Ti, Liu Fen and Lu Xun; his tributes to revolutionary and patriotic fighters; and his verse on the people as makers of history.

Wang's central argument is that Mao's heroism develops from individual self-confidence into a materialist view of history. Early lines such as 'Rebuking the warlords of the day as dung' show a young man's resolve to save the nation, which led him to Marxism after the May Fourth Movement. Wang reads the lines on emperors such as Qin Shihuang and Genghis Khan, and on slave and peasant rebel leaders, as a critique of the old history centred on kings and generals. The poems honouring Huang Gonglue, Peng Dehuai, Yang Kaihui, Luo Ronghuan, Ding Ling, Dai An'lan and the Nanjing Road 'Good Eighth Company' show a revolutionary pantheon. Wang then claims that Mao's 'people-centred view of history' holds the masses to be the true heroes, citing the line that 'the people of the proletariat' are the 'heroes of today'.

Wang concludes that after 1949 Mao's poetry turned to celebrating the builders of the new China and a new generation, while keeping its confidence in a people who 'fear neither ... nor'. The people's standpoint is presented as both the theoretical foundation of Mao Zedong Thought and the emotional tone of his verse. Read the original if you want a short, Party-press survey of how Mao's poems are interpreted as expressions of heroism and the people's role in history, with many of the lines and figures identified.
quoteEn: Mao Zedong had a strong heroic complex, yet firmly opposed the heroic view of history.
quoteZh: 毛泽东有浓郁的英雄情结，但坚决反对英雄史观。

glossary.explanation: A conception that history is driven chiefly by great individuals such as rulers and generals. Marxist historiography, as presented in the article, opposes it with the view that the masses make history.
The view, emphasised in Chinese Marxist writing, that the people are the decisive force in historical development.
The Chinese Communist Party's official term for Mao's theories and policies, adapted from Marxism-Leninism to Chinese conditions.

t: Socialism with Chinese characteristics has created a new form of human civilization
zh: 中国特色社会主义创造了人类文明新形态
source: Chinese Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 29 August 2022
paras: This short commentary from 2022 takes up the claim, first made explicitly by Xi Jinping at the celebration of the Communist Party's centenary, that socialism with Chinese characteristics has created a new form of human civilization. Liu Jianjun argues that the claim is both a political declaration and an academic proposition that needs scholarly explanation. In Liu's account, it expresses the Party's confidence in the path, theory, system and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics.

The article first traces how civilization discourse, latent in the Marxist classics, became explicit and systematic among Chinese communists after reform and opening up. It then clarifies concepts: civilization versus culture, civilization form versus social formation, and the place of socialist civilization within a communist civilization that is to surpass private-property civilizations. Finally it sets out three dimensions in which the new form can be understood.

Liu holds that every social formation is also a civilization form, and that socialism with Chinese characteristics is a more specific form within socialist civilization. It is a complete civilization form because it unites path, theory, system and culture, and also material, political, spiritual, social and ecological civilization. Liu calls it complex and "atypical", to be grasped through three combined dimensions: a new form of Chinese civilization (its modern form, arising in a period of renewal), of modern civilization (a path to modernization different from the West's, described as a contemporary or surpassing form), and of socialist civilization (its Chinese form, achieved by a large, historically old but relatively backward Eastern country).

Liu concludes that this civilization form enriches the diversity of world civilizations, promotes exchange and mutual learning, and advances and leads human civilization. It is still developing and will show a clearer outline and a more mature form in future. Read the original if you want a concise statement of how Party theorists conceptually define the "new form of human civilization" formula.
quoteEn: In sum, the civilization form of socialism with Chinese characteristics is the product of the combined creation of Chinese civilization, modern civilization and socialist civilization.
quoteZh: 总之,中国特色社会主义文明形态是中华文明、现代化文明和社会主义文明综合创造的成果。

glossary.explanation: The official name for the Chinese Communist Party's path, theory and system since reform and opening up, combining socialist principles with China's conditions.
A formula Xi Jinping used in 2021 to describe China's path as a distinct contribution to human civilization, beyond the Western model of modernization.
The policy of economic reform and opening to the outside world launched in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping.
A Marxist term for the type of society defined by its mode of production, such as slave, feudal or capitalist society. The author treats each as also a civilization form.

t: The political-ethical dimension of common prosperity
zh: 共同富裕的政治伦理之维
paras: Distributive justice, Wen Changchun notes, is a perennial theme of political philosophy, and the questions of what is distributed, by whom and how shape the contested ground of contemporary political ethics. This commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in July 2022, argues that common prosperity, described as an essential requirement of socialism and a defining feature of Chinese modernization, overcomes four ethical dilemmas that Western modernity could not resolve.

The article is organised around four pairs of values: the individual and the collective, freedom and equality, fairness and efficiency, and government and market. For each pair, Wen first sets out what the author presents as the Western approach, drawing on liberalism, utilitarianism and economists such as Arthur Okun, and then contrasts it with the Chinese conception of common prosperity. Marx, Engels, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping are cited in support.

On the first two pairs, Wen contends that Western individualism and negative liberty make wealth an exclusive private good, defended through formal equality of opportunity and leading to polarisation between rich and poor. Chinese culture, in the author's account, is group-centred, so that prosperity is shared. Common prosperity permits some people and regions to get rich first, but is not egalitarianism: it seeks substantive equality, with no one left behind. On the third and fourth pairs, Wen argues that fairness must not be sacrificed to efficiency, nor efficiency to fairness, and that material wealth must go together with spiritual and cultural richness. Western societies are said to leave distribution as an afterthought to capital's logic and to favour the market over the state, whereas China combines an effective market with a capable government. Wen sets out three tiers of distribution: primary distribution by the market, redistribution by the state through taxes, social security and transfers, and a third distribution through charity and voluntary giving.

Wen concludes that China has entered an era of gradually realising common prosperity for all the people, and that this conception of prosperity has produced a Chinese modernization distinct from the Western one. In the author's view, it effectively overcomes and dissolves the political-ethical predicaments of Western modernity. Read the original if you want a concise example of how Chinese academic commentary in 2022 framed common prosperity as a normative alternative to Western political philosophy.
quoteEn: Common prosperity does not mean simultaneous prosperity, but encourages and allows some people and some regions to take the lead on the road to wealth.
quoteZh: 共同富裕并不是同步富裕，而是鼓励和允许一部分人、一部分地区在致富道路上先行一步。

glossary.explanation: A goal of shared affluence for all, long associated with socialism in Chinese official discourse. It has been emphasised again since the early 2020s, especially in policy on income gaps and distribution.
The official name for China's path of modernization, presented as distinct from Western models. It was formally elaborated by the Party in 2021–2022.
A concept referring to distribution through charity, donations and voluntary mutual aid, supplementing market-based primary distribution and state redistribution.

t: The contemporary value of whole-process people's democracy
zh: 全过程人民民主的时代价值
paras: This short commentary, first published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today on 15 June 2022, asks what whole-process people's democracy contributes in the present era. Zhou argues that it takes the people's position as masters of the country as the essence of democracy, grows out of China's own history and conditions, and at the same time expresses a democratic aspiration shared by all humanity. In Zhou's account it also enriches the forms of human political civilization.

The article has three parts. The first traces the roots of this democracy in modern Chinese history, in the Party's institutional building and in traditional culture. The second describes its practical features and the sense of gain it gives ordinary people, set against Western electoral democracy. The third presents its contribution to socialist democratic theory and to other countries, particularly late-developing ones.

Zhou's central claim is that this democracy is more complete than Western models. Western systems, in the author's reading, give citizens the vote but leave policy to interest groups and lobbyists, so that the people are 'awake' only at elections. Whole-process people's democracy is instead described as covering the whole chain (election, consultation, decision-making, management and supervision), all areas of life, and all levels from centre to grassroots. Zhou says this joins procedural and substantive democracy, and direct and indirect democracy, and rests on public ownership as the basis of the economy. As evidence the article cites survey figures on satisfaction with the Chinese government and on views of US democracy, and lists channels such as hearings, deputies' liaison offices and online participation.

Zhou concludes that democratic development should follow a country's own characteristics and reality, which the author calls a basic lesson of China's experience. The article claims that this approach has raised governance capacity, produced economic and social stability, and given other developing countries confidence in finding their own paths, offering 'Chinese wisdom' to world political civilization. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the official case for whole-process people's democracy was framed for a general readership in 2022.
quoteEn: Insisting that China's democracy be designed and developed according to China's characteristics and realities, and unswervingly following a path of democratic development suited to national conditions, is a basic experience of China's democratic development.
quoteZh: 坚持中国的民主按照中国的特点、中国的实际来设计和发展，坚定不移走符合国情的民主发展之路，是中国民主发展的一条基本经验

glossary.explanation: A concept in official Chinese political discourse, associated with Xi Jinping from 2019, describing China's democracy as covering every stage from election to supervision. Officials present it as an alternative to Western electoral democracy.

t: Promoting win-win development through exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations
zh: 在文明交流互鉴中推动共赢发展
paras: Thierry Meynard, a French sinologist and professor of philosophy at Sun Yat-sen University, offers a personal commentary (originally published in the China Social Sciences Today in August 2022) on how cultures can learn from one another. Drawing on his years of living and teaching in China, he argues that exchange among civilizations should be open, plural and mutually beneficial, leading to what he calls win-win development.

The piece begins with Meynard's impressions of progress since reform and opening up, especially in education, and notes that he joined Sun Yat-sen University in 2006 after doctoral study at Peking University in the 1990s. He then sets out three principles for his academic work, drawing on history, his teaching and his reading of the philosopher Liang Shuming. It closes with remarks on the pandemic and China's growing international educational influence.

Meynard's three principles are: understand Chinese cultural traditions deeply and avoid applying Western values directly to China; encourage interaction between teacher and student; and avoid a simple opposition between Western and Chinese thought. Following Liang Shuming, he favours a triangular structure that includes Indian Buddhism, and says that dialogue should extend to the Arab world, Africa and Latin America. He cites early Jesuit-era exchange, such as Chinese examinations influencing Europe and the Xu Guangqi–Matteo Ricci translation of Euclid, as cases where both sides benefited. He observes that foreign philosophy in China remains mostly European and American, and links the ideal of great harmony (datong) to respect for difference.

Meynard concludes that China should be both open to other cultures and distinctive in its own, and that Chinese culture is both national and global. He cites the numbers of Confucius Institutes and international students as signs of rising influence, and expresses his belief that China can open a model path for exchange and mutual learning among diverse civilizations. Read the original if you want a foreign scholar's personal, broadly favourable view of China's educational and cultural exchange, framed through Liang Shuming and Sino-Western intellectual history.
quoteEn: Academic exchange should have a triangular structure, an idea I also owe to Mr Liang Shuming.
quoteZh: 学术交流应该是一个三角结构，我的这个想法也是受到梁漱溟先生的启发。

glossary.explanation: The policy launched in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping, introducing market-oriented economic reforms and opening China to foreign trade and investment.
A classical Confucian ideal of a harmonious world community, found in the Book of Rites and later invoked by modern thinkers and official discourse.
Chinese-language and culture centres established abroad since 2004 with Chinese government support, usually in partnership with local universities.

t: Shifts in human civilization and the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind
zh: 人类文明变局与“人类命运共同体”理念
paras: Liu Liangjian takes up the idea of a community with a shared future for mankind, which the author presents as an important contribution China has made in recent years. Liu argues that it is also a generative concept that could become a breakthrough point for innovation in Chinese philosophical discourse. The question "where is the world heading?" is described as both a practical issue of global governance and one of the most basic philosophical questions of the age.

The short commentary, originally published in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in August 2022, begins with a sketch of world civilizations. It runs from the rough balance among Europe, the Middle East, India and China before the mid-nineteenth century to Western dominance afterwards, and then to the May Fourth Movement of 1919. It then turns to the philosophical foundations of the concept and to its implications for world political order.

Liu holds that the world is entering a new "cultural germination period" in which different civilizations interact on Chinese soil. Drawing on Feng Qi's formulation of China's basic modern question, Liu reframes the contemporary question as where Chinese and human civilization are heading amid the "compression of time and space". This requires a "contemporary" view of time and history distinct from ancient and modern ones. Liu suggests "global-locality" as a political concept for a world moving beyond nation-states, with a world government as centre that still accommodates plurality. The idea is also tied to the ancient ideal of great harmony (datong), to a Marxist view of world history and to traditional Chinese emphasis on harmony.

Liu concludes that the community with a shared future for mankind should be built up in theory on a philosophy of history grounded in a rich concept of "contemporaneity". Because it includes nature and "heaven", it aims to let people realise their nature within a community of heaven and humanity. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a Chinese philosopher links this official concept to Feng Qi, Confucian ideas and world-historical theory.
quoteEn: The basic question for contemporary China becomes: against the background of "time-space compression", where are Chinese civilization and human civilization heading?
quoteZh: 当代中国的基本问题演变为：在“时空压缩”的背景下，中国文明及人类文明向何处去？

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: A foreign-policy and theoretical concept promoted by Xi Jinping since around 2012–13. It calls for countries to treat their interests as interdependent and to pursue shared development and global governance.
A Confucian ideal of a world in which "the world is shared by all", drawn from the Book of Rites. Modern thinkers such as Kang Youwei revived it as a utopian vision.

keywords: community with a shared future for mankind

t: Distinctive features of China's five thousand years of civilisation
zh: 中华五千年文明的特质
paras: This short commentary, first published in China Social Sciences Today in August 2022, asks what marks out Chinese civilisation over five thousand years. Liu Qingzhu argues that it is distinguished by continuity without rupture and by an inclusiveness summed up in the phrase "yourong nai da" (tolerance makes greatness).

Liu starts from Engels's remark that the state is a summary of civilised society, and from Yi Jianping's etymological claim that "civilisation is the state". The author treats the state's material carriers as its people, its territory and the people's shared idea of the state. The text first applies an archaeological reading of non-rupture to each of the three, then turns to inclusiveness, internal and external.

On continuity, Liu cites genetic studies showing that most people in China today are genetically close to populations of the middle Yellow River valley five thousand years ago. Liu adds that 99 per cent of surnames derive from the Yan-Huang lineage system. The author traces a stable territory from the Miaodigou culture to the Qin-Han dominions. Shared identity is shown in the idea of "zhong" (centrality) and "zhonghe" (harmony): capitals, Liu says, were sited at the "centre" from the Xishuipo tomb onward, expressing fairness towards all quarters. On inclusiveness, Liu points to non-Han dynasties such as the Northern Wei, Liao, Jin, Yuan and Qing, which are regarded as part of Chinese civilisation, and contrasts the Silk Road with the colonialism of the Age of Discovery.

Liu concludes that these features, continuous people, land and identity together with an inclusive outlook, explain the vitality of Chinese civilisation. The Silk Road, in the author's account, shows friendship and cooperation rather than colonial expansion. Read the original if you want a brief example of how a leading Chinese archaeologist presents the continuity of Chinese civilisation in official-style terms.
quoteEn: The \"vitality\" of the unbroken continuity of five thousand years of Chinese civilisation lies in the idea of \"tolerance makes greatness\" held by its state and its people.
quoteZh: 中华五千年文明“不断裂”的“生命力”，在于其国家与国民的“有容乃大”的理念。

glossary.literal: having capacity for inclusion, one becomes great
glossary.explanation: A classical Chinese saying about the greatness that comes from broad-mindedness. Here it is used to characterise Chinese civilisation's inclusiveness towards ethnic groups and other countries.
A concept from classical Confucian thought about balance and harmony. The author links it to the siting of capitals at the "centre" and to the ideal of fairness towards all quarters.

glossary.literal: descendants of the Yan and Yellow emperors
glossary.explanation: A traditional self-designation of the Chinese people as descendants of the legendary Yan Emperor and Yellow Emperor, who are regarded as founding ancestors.

t: Cultural identity and Chinese civilization amid great changes in the world
zh: 文化认同与世界大变局中的中国文明
source: China Social Sciences Today (Zhongguo shehui kexue bao), 30 August 2022
paras: Li Yuji takes up the claim, made by some Western scholars such as Lucian W. Pye, that China is "a civilization pretending to be a state". Li reads this as showing both a vague Western grasp of how civilization, state and nation relate in ancient China and the real uniqueness of that relationship. The article, a short newspaper commentary, argues that Chinese civilization is distinctive in combining national, state and cultural identity in a "trinity", and that this helps China in today's globalization.

The piece begins with the origins of Chinese civilization, then looks at the Xia, Shang and Zhou dynasties and the Spring and Autumn period. It turns to Confucian thought as an expression of this trinity. It ends with the contemporary era of modernization and globalization.

Li traces the trinity to China's particular agricultural environment and to a prehistoric faith centred on ancestor deities. In Li's account, this faith was this-worldly and tied to kinship and territory, and it blocked the rise of a transcendent universal god. Cultural identity therefore became the basis of national and state identity, as shown by the slogan "revere the king, expel the barbarians" and by the pairing of saving the nation and saving the state in modern times. Li credits Confucianism with fusing these elements, and lists openness, compatibility and the state's duty to protect its people as traits that let Chinese civilization survive repeated conflicts and divisions.

Li concludes that these traits help China avoid the cultural contradictions and civilizational conflicts that Li says trap some non-Western countries torn between modernization and localization. Li lists five advantages, including openness, ethnic and religious compatibility, a practical work ethic, strong state backing, and vitality in building a "new form of human civilization". Li holds that China is following a path suited to its own traditions and circumstances. Read the original if you want a brief example of how Chinese scholars use the civilization-state idea to argue for the continuity of Chinese culture.
quoteEn: Chinese civilization has a trinitarian character in national, state and cultural identity, a character that derives from China's particular livelihood environment and the distinctive path by which its civilization originated.
quoteZh: 中国文明在民族、国家、文化认同上具有三位一体的特征，这种特征来源于中国特殊的生业环境与文明起源的独特路径。

t: How the Party served the interests of the masses in the Central Soviet Area period
zh: 中央苏区时期党如何为群众谋利益
paras: This short commentary, first published in Study Times, asks how the Party worked for the interests of ordinary people in the Central Soviet Area. Zhu and Huang argue that the Party came to see protection of mass interests as the foundation of revolutionary victory. They point to the call of the provisional central government of the Chinese Soviet Republic to represent the poorest workers and peasants "wholeheartedly".

The article covers three areas of practice: political structure, economic work and social welfare. It draws on examples from the Soviet organs, land reform, cooperatives, public health, relief and education, with figures from Jiangxi and Fujian, especially Guangchang county.

On politics, the authors hold that protecting political rights was the basis for all other rights. They cite the Soviet Organic Law, which gave voting rights to non-exploiting men and women aged 16 and over, and report that women made up over 25 per cent of delegates in Jiangxi's elections. On the economy, they say land distribution made peasants masters of the land. Cooperatives then eased shortages of labour, oxen, seed and capital; by March 1933 the authors count 1,423 cooperatives in 17 counties. On social work, they describe mass hygiene campaigns, mutual aid societies and donation drives for relief, and Lenin primary schools, night schools and literacy classes. In Guangchang, they report 124 such primary schools by the end of 1933.

The authors conclude that these measures improved livelihoods, raised political enthusiasm and won peasant support. They describe relief work under wartime scarcity as a direct sign of the advanced character of a Marxist party. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed account of Central Soviet Area governance, with local statistics, as presented in a Party newspaper.
quoteEn: In the Central Soviet Area period, despite wartime shortages of funds, the Party and the Soviet government still found ways to relieve people in hardship, which is a direct expression of the advanced character of a Marxist party.
quoteZh: 中央苏区时期，面临经费不足的战争环境，党和苏维埃政府仍然想方设法开展对困难群众的救济，这是马克思主义政党先进性的直观体现。

glossary.explanation: The main Communist-held revolutionary base in southern Jiangxi and western Fujian in the early 1930s. It was the seat of the Chinese Soviet Republic, founded in 1931.
The government proclaimed by the Chinese Communist Party in November 1931 in the Central Soviet Area. It lasted until the Red Army's Long March in 1934.

t: Mao Zedong's far-reaching considerations in editing Party history document collections in the Yan'an period
zh: 延安时期毛泽东主持编辑党史文献集的深远考虑
paras: Why did Mao Zedong personally lead the compilation of a series of Party history and theory collections during the Yan'an period (1938–1945)? Wan Ruijia and Zou Weishao argue that the work was a deliberate political and ideological undertaking, not merely archival. In their account it was meant to unify the Party's thinking, summarise its historical experience and change its work style, and it is presented as a tradition of the Chinese Communist Party that began at Yan'an.

The article is organised in three parts. The first describes the collections Mao edited and sorts them into three types: political documents (Since the Sixth Congress, Before the Sixth Congress, Two Lines), writings of the Marxist classics (Methodology of Thought of Marx, Engels, Lenin and Stalin; Lenin, Stalin and the Comintern on China), and investigation material (Rural Surveys). The second part sets out Mao's reasons, and the third assesses the effects of the collections.

For the authors, the context was the stalemate phase of the War of Resistance, the Wannan Incident (1941) and the lack of agreement inside the Party about past 'Left' and Right errors. They identify three purposes. The first was to unify thinking before the long-delayed Seventh Party Congress, linking the collections to the Rectification Movement. The second was to give cadres original documents with which to tell right from wrong, above all about Wang Ming's 'Left' dogmatist line. The third was to change the Party's style, tackling dogmatism and the separation of theory from practice, and promoting investigation and research.

The authors conclude that the collections helped bring the Party 'unprecedentedly' together under Mao's banner and established the guiding position of Mao Zedong Thought. They also supplied the documentary and methodological basis for the Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party, and encouraged a style of linking theory with practice, ties with the masses and self-criticism. They claim that without these collections the Resolution would have been hard to produce. Read the original if you study the Rectification Movement, Party document compilation or the Party's own account of Mao's role in Yan'an.
quoteEn: Editing these Party history document collections played an extremely important role in unifying understanding within the Party, unifying the thinking of the whole Party, further strengthening Party spirit and promoting Party unity.
quoteZh: 编辑这些党史文献集，对统一党内认识、统一全党思想、进一步增强党性和增进党的团结，起到了极为重要的作用。

glossary.explanation: A Party-wide education and discipline campaign launched in 1942 and aimed at subjectivism, sectarianism and 'Party formalism'. It consolidated Mao Zedong's leadership.
In Party discourse, applying Marxist texts and foreign models mechanically without regard to Chinese conditions. Mao's camp attached the label to Wang Ming and his associates.
The congress held in Yan'an in 1945, after repeated postponement. It enshrined Mao Zedong Thought in the Party constitution.

glossary.zh: 关于若干历史问题的决议
glossary.pinyin: guānyú ruògān lìshǐ wèntí de juéyì
glossary.en: Resolution on Certain Questions in the History of Our Party
glossary.explanation: A 1945 Central Committee resolution that assessed the Party's history up to that point, criticised the earlier 'Left' lines and affirmed Mao's leadership.
The January 1941 clash in which Nationalist forces attacked the Communist-led New Fourth Army. It put the Second United Front under severe strain.

t: Let the lamp of the Chinese spirit shine on the literary and artistic peaks of the new era
zh: 让中国精神的灯火在新时代的文艺高峰上闪亮
paras: Writing in Qiushi in 2022, Tie Ning asks what it takes for Chinese literature and art to reach new peaks in the new era. The essay marks the eighth anniversary of Xi Jinping's Talk at the Forum on Literature and Art (2014). It also recalls Xi's call in December 2021 for literary masters and peaks. Tie's answer is that writers and artists should be guided by three fundamental ideas: the times, the people and innovation.

The essay is a reflective address in an essayistic, personal register rather than a systematic study. It moves from Beijing's long cultural history, through Cao Xueqin and Lu Xun, to modern and contemporary writers such as Zhou Libo, Liu Qing and Ma Feng. It then turns to recent works: the television drama Shanhai qing (Ocean of Mountains and Seas), the dance-drama Zhi ci qinglü and the Beijing Winter Olympics ceremonies. Each of the three keywords is anchored in a few such examples and in quotations from Xi.

On the times, Tie argues that writers must grasp the historical position of the new era and combine an eagle's overview with the rootedness of a tree in everyday life. Citing Zhou Libo's Great Changes in a Mountain Village and Liu Qing's fourteen years in a village, Tie calls for "historical initiative": writers should join the people's historical practice rather than merely observe it. On the people, Tie reads Xi's remark that the people are not an abstract symbol as a theoretical innovation, describing a dialectical movement from the concrete to the whole and back. On innovation, Tie presents the "guochao" works as creative transformation and innovative development of excellent traditional Chinese culture.

Tie concludes that the new era needs and can produce literary masters. Tie sketches a second, spiritual "central axis" of Beijing, formed by generations of writers and artists, which binds people together emotionally. The closing hope is that the lamp of the Chinese spirit will shine on the new era's artistic peaks. Read the original if you want to see how a senior figure in China's official literary institutions applies Xi Jinping's cultural directives to creative work, or if you are interested in the rhetoric of the Chinese literary establishment in 2022.
quoteEn: The people are both the source and the purpose of literature and art, and also its fundamental method.
quoteZh: 人民既是文艺的源泉和目的，也是文艺的根本方法

glossary.explanation: A Party term for consciously taking part in and driving historical change. Tie uses it for writers who see their work as part of the people's making of history.
A popular term for fashionable products and artworks that fuse traditional Chinese elements with contemporary style.

keywords: Talk at the Forum on Literature and Art

t: The background and course of the Project to Trace the Origins of Chinese Civilization
zh: 中华文明探源工程的“来龙去脉”
paras: Published in Study Times (Xuexi Shibao) in 2022, this short explanatory piece follows the 39th collective study session of the Political Bureau (27 May 2022), which was devoted to deepening the Project to Trace the Origins of Chinese Civilization. Dai Sheng asks what the project is, and what its aims, stages, value and significance are. The author's answer is that it is a long-running, multidisciplinary national undertaking whose first 20 years have produced substantial but only preliminary and stage-specific results.

The article opens with Xi Jinping's remarks at the study session and then moves through three parts. The first explains how the project grew out of the Xia-Shang-Zhou Chronology Project (1996–2000). The second walks through the project's phases from the pre-study of 2001–2003 to the fifth phase of 2020–2024. The third sets out the results announced in 2018, the related "Archaeology China" programme launched in 2017, and the tasks ahead.

Dai's account stresses how the project's scope widened. The chronology project, the author says, was meant to answer overseas scholars who denied the Xia dynasty because documented dates reach back only to 841 BCE. The origins project then extended its time range from 2500 BCE to 3500 BCE. Its geography grew from the Central Plains to the Yellow and Yangtze valleys, the West Liao River basin and the border regions. Its content grew from archaeological periodization and settlement patterns to environment, subsistence, resources and spiritual life. The author lists three achievements. These are the dating of the early emergence of civilization (signs around 5800 years ago, entry into the civilizational stage from 5300 years ago, a mature Central Plains form around 3800 years ago); a picture of diverse regional paths within a pattern of pluralistic unity; and a Chinese standard for judging civilization that goes beyond the Western "three elements" of metallurgy, writing and cities.

Dai concludes that the work ahead is heavy. The author lists future tasks: study more regions, push back to 8,000 or even 10,000 years ago, deepen theory, popularize the findings, and build a discipline, academic and discourse system with Chinese characteristics, style and manner. The piece repeats Xi's call for coordinated planning and joint work between archaeology, history, and the humanities and natural sciences. Read the original if you want a compact official-style chronology of the project's phases, leaders and announced findings, or if you want to see how Party media present the project's scholarly and political aims.
quoteEn: The Project to Trace the Origins of Chinese Civilization is a systematic undertaking of great academic value, which must be advanced in an organized and planned way and carried out over the long term.
quoteZh: 中华文明探源工程是一项学术价值重大，需要有组织有计划推进，长期开展的系统工程。

glossary.en: Project to Trace the Origins of Chinese Civilization
glossary.explanation: A state-backed multidisciplinary research programme, formally titled "Comprehensive Study of the Origins and Early Development of Chinese Civilization". It was approved in 2001, began in 2002, and has run in successive phases.
A national project (1996–2000) to build a firm chronology for the Xia, Shang and Western Zhou periods. It used humanities and natural-science methods together.
A framework, associated with the anthropologist Fei Xiaotong, in which Chinese civilization is seen as formed from many regional cultures converging into a unified whole.

A major archaeology programme launched by the National Cultural Heritage Administration in 2017. It covers human origins, the origins of civilization and the formation of a unified multi-ethnic state.

t: Mao Zedong's thought on investigation and research in his family letters of the early People's Republic
zh: 新中国成立初期毛泽东家书中的调查研究思想探究
source: Research on Marxist Theory in Colleges and Universities (高校马克思主义理论研究)
paras: Yang Xinbin asks how Mao Zedong's habit of social investigation and research (diaoyan) continued after 1949, when he could no longer carry out fieldwork as he had before. The article argues that, between the founding of the People's Republic and the socialist transformation, Mao used letters to and from relatives as a special information channel. In Yang's reading, these letters served a function close to investigation and research and carried forward his earlier methods.

The article draws on 46 published letters from 1949 to 1953, sent to 32 recipients among his paternal, maternal and wife's kin. Most of these were peasants, small producers, local cadres and intellectuals in rural Hunan. It has three parts: the historical setting of the family-letter route, the major problems Mao raised in the letters, and the principles of investigation they reveal.

Yang links three recurring concerns in the letters to national policy. Grain shortages in 1950 are traced to wartime requisitions and a fiscal system not yet unified, which Mao answered by lowering requisition rates and unifying finance. Complaints about local work in 1950 are tied to coercive cadre conduct and the Party's rapid growth, which prompted rectification campaigns. Grain shortages in 1952 are read as showing the fragility of smallholder farming after land reform, and so as supporting Mao's push towards agricultural cooperation. Yang then identifies four principles in the letters. These are the people's standing as the subject of practice, typical-case analysis ("dissecting a sparrow"), the investigation meeting, and winning the trust of those surveyed. Kinship, Yang argues, made candid reporting more likely.

Yang concludes that Mao's attention to family letters continued his pre-1949 approach and was an attempt to keep up the Party's good traditions while in power. The article presents investigation and research as a Party heirloom and calls for it to be inherited in the new era, in service of the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation. Read the original if you are interested in Mao's working methods, in Hunan rural conditions in the early 1950s, or in how Chinese scholars use private correspondence as evidence of policy thinking.
quoteEn: Mao Zedong's emphasis on family letters is consistent in spirit with his investigative art of \"making friends\" with the masses.
quoteZh: 毛泽东重视家书，和与群众“做朋友”的调查艺术在精神上是一致的。

glossary.explanation: A Party working method of gathering first-hand information from the grassroots before making policy. Mao Zedong promoted it from the 1930s, and it remains a staple of Party rhetoric.
Campaigns to correct ideological errors and bad working styles among Party members. The Yan'an campaign of 1942 is the best-known example; another was launched in 1950.
The redistribution of landlords' land to peasants, carried out in newly liberated areas of China from 1950 to 1952.
The step-by-step organisation of individual peasant households into mutual-aid teams and cooperatives in the 1950s. It was the route to the socialist transformation of agriculture.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The official national goal, closely associated with Xi Jinping's slogan of the Chinese Dream.

t: The effects of developing the rural collective economy in the period of agricultural collectivisation and their lessons
zh: 农业集体化时期发展农村集体经济的效用及其启示
source: Studies on Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping Theories, 2022 no. 4
paras: Wu Shuli asks how rural revitalisation can overcome the weakness of fragmented smallholder farming ("dispersal") while drawing on the strength of a new type of collective economy ("unification"). The article argues that this question cannot be understood without tracing the history of rural collective ownership. Wu contends that the collective economy of the collectivisation period (c. 1951–1983) achieved real economic and social results, and that its experience offers guidance for today's "three rural issues" (agriculture, rural areas, farmers).

Wu begins by criticising existing scholarship for three tendencies: stigmatising collective economy as inefficient and uniform, separating the collective era from the household contract responsibility system, and concentrating on political campaigns rather than everyday economic development. The article then has three parts: why the Party promoted collective economy, what it concretely achieved, and what lessons follow for the present. The evidence includes statistics, Mao Zedong's statements, local cases such as Shandong's Yantai and Henan's Shibanyan supply and marketing cooperative, and the views of foreign scholars such as Theda Skocpol.

In Wu's account, collectivisation was needed for socialist industrialisation, for raising agricultural productivity, and for keeping a socialist direction in the countryside. Wu credits collective organisation with pooling land and labour, expanding mechanisation and irrigation, supporting commune and brigade enterprises that later fed township and village enterprises, running supply and marketing cooperatives, and providing schooling, cooperative medical care and the "five guarantees". Wu also credits it with reshaping farmers' political participation, values and family life. Wu concedes problems, including the price scissors between industry and agriculture, weak property and distribution rules, and tensions between administrative orders and farmers' voluntarism, but denies that these amount to the failure of the collective system.

For the present, Wu proposes developing collective economy in forms suited to local conditions, on a voluntary basis and without "rushing" or mass campaigns, so that smallholders are linked to modern agriculture rather than eliminated. Wu also calls for collective channels and supply and marketing reform to reduce smallholders' exposure to merchant capital. Finally, Wu argues for Party branch leadership so that capital serves farmers and common prosperity is not undermined, citing Tangyue in Guizhou and Yantai as examples. Read the original if you want a favourable reassessment of the collective era, with historical detail and policy implications for rural revitalisation, from a Chinese academic perspective.
quoteEn: Dispelling the prejudice that "collective organisations are inefficient" and developing and strengthening a new type of rural collective economy is an important part of rural revitalisation.
quoteZh: 破除“集体组织效率不高”的偏见，发展壮大新型农村集体经济，是乡村振兴的重要一环。

glossary.explanation: A standard shorthand in Chinese policy for agriculture, rural areas and farmers, treated as a single priority area of government work.
The post-1978 system in which collectively owned land is contracted to individual households, which farm it and keep output beyond state and collective quotas.
A national strategy launched in 2017 to promote rural industry, ecology, culture, governance and living standards.
Rural enterprises run by people's communes and production brigades; they were the forerunners of the township and village enterprises of the reform era.
A Chinese goal of shared prosperity for all, emphasised in official policy under Xi Jinping.

t: Practical explorations in China's forestry development, 1949–1966
zh: 1949—1966年我国林业建设的实践探索
paras: Ren Ling asks how the Communist Party built up forestry in the first seventeen years of the People's Republic, starting from a country that, according to the author, had forest cover of only 8.6% in 1949. The article argues that this period laid the foundations of forestry work and that, by 1966, China had begun to find its own path of forestry development. It holds that this experience still offers lessons for forestry work and for building an ecological civilization today.

The article runs from 1949 to the national forestry work conference of February 1966, which it treats as a historical turning point. It is organised in three parts: the leadership and the actors of forestry construction; the policy of protecting, planting and tending forests while harvesting and using them rationally; and the regulations, forest ownership rights and tree-planting funds that supported this work. Ren draws mainly on Party and State Council directives, ministerial regulations, and remarks by Mao Zedong, Chen Yun, Liu Shaoqi, Zhou Enlai and others.

Ren's first main point is that Party committees at each level were made responsible for forestry. Mass mobilisation under the mass line, state forest farms and specialised training institutions supplied the planters, the labour force and the expertise. Second, the founding guideline of 1950 was "universal forest protection, key-area afforestation, rational felling and use". It was adjusted over time by timber-saving measures, comprehensive use of wood and scientific research, and after the Great Leap Forward, which Ren says caused predatory logging. Third, institutional arrangements settled ownership and funding. These included the principle "whoever plants owns" (1961), a distinction between state, collective and individual forests, and a forest-nurturing fund drawn from timber sales costs. Ren says these steps tried to link ownership, management and income so as to protect peasants' enthusiasm for forestry.

Ren concludes that by 1966 China had over 200 million mu of young plantations, more than 3,500 state forest farms and an annual planting capacity of about 40 million mu, according to the article's figures. The author credits the Party's leadership, the mass line and analysis of specific problems for these results, and holds that these lessons still bear on forestry work and ecological civilization today. Read the original if you want a detailed, document-based account of early People's Republic forestry policy, ownership rules and funding mechanisms as presented in Party-history scholarship.
quoteEn: In this way, the state forests had people to manage them, and forest-area workers also had an incentive to raise their output and income.
quoteZh: 这样，国家森林有人管理，林区职工也有了生产增收的动力。

glossary.explanation: An official Chinese policy concept, prominent since the 2010s, that makes environmental protection part of national development goals. The article links historical forestry work to it.
A Party method of work that stresses drawing on and mobilising ordinary people. Here it describes campaigns to involve the public in planting and protecting trees.
A 1961 principle that newly planted trees belong to whoever planted them (state, commune, team or individual). It aimed to restore incentives for tree planting.
A special fund drawn from timber sales costs and reserved for forest renewal, planting and tending. It was meant to let forestry finance itself.
The 1958 mass campaign for rapid industrial and agricultural growth, which included backyard steel-making and communal canteens. The article says it led to heavy logging.

t: Grasping the milestone significance of the great transformations of the past decade in the new era
zh: 深刻把握新时代十年伟大变革的里程碑意义
paras: Published in Guangming Daily on 25 August 2022, shortly before the 20th Party Congress, this commentary by Zhong Xiaowu explains Xi Jinping's statement that the great transformations of the past ten years in the new era are of milestone significance. Xi made the statement in a speech to a study session for provincial and ministerial leaders. Zhong argues that, since the 18th Party Congress (2012), the Party Central Committee with Xi at its core has produced historic achievements and historic changes. In this account, China's development now stands at a new historical starting point.

The article is organised around the areas in which Zhong sees these changes. It moves from the Party itself to the economy and the first centenary goal, then to reform, the road of socialism with Chinese characteristics and institutional development. It then turns to theory, Chinese modernization and global initiatives, and finally to the Chinese nation, ethnic unity and traditional culture. Zhong places the decade within the history of the Party, the People's Republic, reform and opening up, socialism and the Chinese nation.

On the Party, Zhong argues that its leadership has been comprehensively strengthened. The author cites the Two Establishes, the Two Upholds, the campaign against corruption and the Party's self-reform as the means by which the Party found a path out of the historical cycle of rise and decline. On the economy, Zhong cites GDP above 100 trillion yuan, per capita GDP above US$10,000, a rise in China's share of the world economy from 11.3% to over 18%, and the lifting of nearly 100 million people out of poverty. Zhong states that a moderately prosperous society has been built in all respects.

Zhong also credits the decade with the creation of Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era, described as Marxism of contemporary China and of the twenty-first century. It is also credited with a Chinese modernization that, in the author's words, breaks the equation of modernization with Westernization and shifts the contest between socialism and capitalism in socialism's favour. The article adds a community with a shared future for mankind and the Belt and Road Initiative. It concludes that the nation is closer than ever to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, which it calls irreversible. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary summarised the achievements of the Xi era on the eve of the 20th Party Congress.
quoteEn: Today we are closer than at any time in history to the goal of the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, and more confident and more capable than at any time in history of achieving it.
quoteZh: 今天，我们比历史上任何时期都更接近中华民族伟大复兴的目标，比历史上任何时期都更有信心、有能力实现这个目标。

glossary.explanation: A formula adopted in the Party's 2021 historical resolution. It affirms Xi Jinping's position as the core of the Party Central Committee and of the whole Party, and the guiding role of his thought.
A Party requirement to uphold the core status of the General Secretary and the authority and centralised, unified leadership of the Party Central Committee.
Official term for the Party's efforts to discipline itself and combat corruption and misconduct. Xi Jinping presents it as the answer to the historical cycle of dynastic rise and decline.
Official term for China's own path to modernization, presented as distinct from Western models. It has been prominent in Party discourse since the 20th Party Congress (2022).

glossary.en: a community with a shared future for mankind
glossary.explanation: Xi Jinping's concept of international relations, centred on common security, development and cooperation among states.
A Chinese international infrastructure and economic cooperation programme launched in 2013.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.literal: great revival of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The Party's central national goal, presented as restoring China's strength and international standing after the 'century of humiliation'.

t: Accurately grasping the profound meaning of the "Two Integrations"
zh: 准确把握“两个结合”的深刻内涵
paras: This commentary, first published in Guangming Daily on 24 August 2022, takes up how to understand the Two Integrations: combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. Xie argues that the formula deepens understanding of the laws governing adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times. Grasping its historical necessity, theoretical logic and practical innovation, the author says, is essential for understanding how Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era took shape. The piece opens by citing Xi Jinping's remarks at a seminar for provincial and ministerial-level leading officials ahead of the 20th Party Congress.

The text is organised in three numbered sections: historical necessity, theoretical logic and practical innovation. The first traces the Party's theoretical achievements from Mao Zedong Thought through Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents and the Scientific Outlook on Development, to Xi Jinping's thought. The second turns to the reception of Marxism in China after the Opium War and the October Revolution. The third addresses the practical orientation of the Two Integrations and what they require today.

Xie's central claim is that Marxism succeeded in China because the Party rooted it in Chinese soil and because it can connect with fine traditional culture. The author cites ideas such as great harmony under heaven and the people as the foundation of the state, which are said to resonate with human emancipation, common prosperity and the free and all-round development of each person. Integration with tradition is described not as repeating particular cultural content but as drawing out its spirit through creative transformation and innovative development. In the article's account, the Party's revolutionary culture and advanced socialist culture share a root with traditional culture, and this underpins the path of Chinese modernization. Theory, Xie says, becomes a material force once the masses grasp it, and the achievements since the 18th Party Congress (2012) are attributed to the guidance of Xi Jinping Thought.

Xie concludes that the Two Integrations must keep developing in step with practice. Contemporary China's social change and practical innovation are said to give them strong momentum and wide scope. The author calls for deep excavation of the ideas and moral essence of traditional culture, reinterpreted with the spirit of the times, so that Chinese civilisation regains its brilliance and Marxism in twenty-first-century China opens new horizons. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary in 2022 framed the Two Integrations just before the 20th Party Congress.
quoteEn: Combining the basic tenets of Marxism with fine traditional Chinese culture does not mean simply repeating specific cultural content; it stresses drawing out the subtle spirit of culture and achieving creative transformation and innovative development.
quoteZh: 马克思主义基本原理同中华优秀传统文化相结合，不是停留在对具体文化内容的简单重复，而是重视文化精神的阐幽发微，实现创造性转化、创新性发展

glossary.explanation: Formula stressing the combination of Marxism's basic tenets with China's specific realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. The second element was added prominently in Xi Jinping's discourse around 2021–2022.

glossary.zh: 马克思主义中国化时代化
glossary.en: adapting Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times
glossary.explanation: Official phrase for the Party's ongoing project of fitting Marxist theory to Chinese conditions and to the contemporary era.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's guiding ideology, written into its constitution in 2017 under Xi Jinping's leadership.
Official term for China's own path of modernization, presented by the Party as distinct from Western models.
Guiding concept associated with Hu Jintao, stressing people-centred, comprehensive and sustainable development.
Theory associated with Jiang Zemin, holding that the Party represents advanced productive forces, advanced culture and the interests of the overwhelming majority.

t: The strategic significance of forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation
zh: 铸牢中华民族共同体意识的战略意义
paras: Writing in Guangming Daily in August 2022, Wang Yanzhong asks why forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation (zhulao Zhonghua minzu gongtongti yishi) should be the main thread of the Party's ethnic work. The author presents it as a major original thesis put forward by the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core, in response to new conditions in ethnic affairs. Wang's answer is that its strategic importance can be understood on five levels: political, theoretical, practical, contemporary and cultural.

The commentary is built as a sequence of five headed sections, each with two sub-points. It draws on Xi Jinping's remarks during an inspection tour of Xinjiang, on the Central United Front Work Conference, on the 2021 Central Conference on Ethnic Work, and on the Party's regulations on united front work. It is a short, programmatic piece that interprets official positions rather than introducing new empirical material.

On the political level, Wang argues that the formulation embodies the Party's overall leadership of ethnic work, now placed within the "large united front work pattern", and keeps that work on course by subordinating ethnic consciousness to the consciousness of the Chinese nation as a community. On the theoretical level, the author calls it the latest result of adapting Marxist ethnic theory to Chinese conditions and a basis for correct views of the nation and of history, one that requires education and countering hostile forces. In practical terms, Wang says it is a guide for ethnic work and a basic principle for handling major relationships, leading to the dialectical unity of commonality and difference. In terms of the times and culture, the author links it to the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, to Chinese and overseas Chinese unity, and to the tradition of "great unity", which Wang says seeks common ground while accepting differences.

Wang concludes that the concept is an inherent requirement of high-quality development in ethnic work and of building a modern socialist country. It is also, in the author's account, the ideological precondition for strengthening the "five identifications", especially identification with Chinese culture, without setting identification with one's own ethnic group against identification with the Chinese nation. Read the original if you want a concise, official-line statement of how Party scholars justify this central concept of current ethnic policy and which documents and formulations they rely on.
quoteEn: Forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation does not mean separating or even opposing identification with one's own ethnic group and identification with the Chinese nation, still less having only the former without the latter; it means jointly building an overall Chinese national identity and jointly promoting the building of the Chinese national community.
quoteZh: 铸牢中华民族共同体意识，不是把对本民族的认同与对中华民族的认同割裂开来甚至对立起来，更不能只有本民族认同没有中华民族认同，而是要共同构建中华民族整体认同，共同促进中华民族共同体建设。

glossary.zh: 铸牢中华民族共同体意识
glossary.en: forging a strong sense of community for the Chinese nation
glossary.literal: cast firm the consciousness of the Chinese nation as a community
glossary.explanation: A formula associated with Xi Jinping, set out at the 2014 Central Conference on Ethnic Work and in the 19th Party Congress report (2017). In 2021 it was declared the main thread of the Party's ethnic work.

Identification with the great motherland, the Chinese nation, Chinese culture, the Communist Party of China and socialism with Chinese characteristics. It is promoted in official ethnic-unity education.
A framework in the Party's united front work regulations that brings ethnic and other work under coordinated leadership by Party committees and the united front department.

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
glossary.literal: great revival of the Chinese nation
glossary.explanation: The Party's central national goal, associated with the Chinese Dream, usually dated to the mid-twenty-first century.
A traditional Chinese political idea of a unified polity. The author reads it as combining unity with diversity.

t: Seeking the code to the success of a century-old Party
zh: 探寻百年大党为什么能够成功的密码
paras: Writing in Guangming Daily in August 2022, Sang Donghua asks why the Communist Party of China has been able to endure and succeed over a hundred years. Taking as his starting point the resolution on the Party's major achievements and historical experience adopted at the Sixth Plenum of the 19th Central Committee (2021), Sang answers that the Party's ideals, original aspiration, fundamental purpose, theoretical character and political courage for self-reform have stayed constant through every change of circumstance.

The article is a short commentary organised into four numbered sections, each describing the Party through a single identity: a mission-driven party, a party of the people, a party armed with scientific theory, and a team of revolutionaries. Each section runs through the revolutionary, socialist-construction, reform-era and post-2012 periods, drawing on quotations from Mao Zedong, Deng Xiaoping and Xi Jinping, on Party documents and on episodes from Party history.

Sang argues that the Party has held to socialism and communism as its goal since its founding in 1921, citing a figure of more than 370 martyrs on record from 1921 to 1949. Its strength, in Sang's account, comes from adhering to a people's standpoint, and Sang points to the Long March story of the shared quilt and to the poverty-alleviation campaign, in which 98.99 million rural poor are said to have been lifted out of poverty under current standards. Sang also credits the Party's ability to adapt Marxism to the Chinese context and the needs of our times, from Mao Zedong Thought to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era. The last strand is self-reform: Sang holds that the Party's greatness lies not in avoiding mistakes but in confronting its own problems, through full and rigorous self-governance of the Party and anti-corruption work.

Sang concludes that the Party's century of history is one of striving for lofty social ideals, of unity with the people, of continuous theoretical innovation, and of using great self-reform to lead great social revolution. These four features are presented as the explanation of why the Party has remained the firm leadership core. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official Party commentary summarises the sources of the Party's success for a general readership in the year of the 20th Party Congress.
quoteEn: The Communist Party of China is great not because it makes no mistakes, but because it never shies away from treating its own ills, faces its own problems squarely, dares to carry out self-reform and dares to remove every virus that erodes the Party's healthy body.
quoteZh: 中国共产党之所以伟大，不在于不犯错误，而在于从不讳疾忌医，直面自身存在的问题，勇于进行自我革命，敢于清除一切侵蚀党的健康肌体的病毒

glossary.en: full and rigorous self-governance of the Party
glossary.literal: comprehensively and strictly govern the Party
glossary.explanation: A slogan associated with Xi Jinping since the 18th Party Congress (2012), covering discipline, anti-corruption and Party-building measures.

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuìzhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party constitution in 2017 and presented as the latest stage in adapting Marxism to China.

t: The Chinese Communist Party's exploration of governing the Party through institutions
zh: 中国共产党制度治党的探索历程
paras: Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in May 2022, Chi Buyun asks how the Chinese Communist Party has come to rely on institutions to govern itself, and how that reliance has developed over a century. Chi defines governing the Party through institutions as the making and enforcement of intra-Party regulations, forming a system that regulates relations inside the Party and between the Party, the state and society. The author argues that this approach is an important support for keeping the Party advanced and for keeping Party building and the Party's cause moving in step.

The short article follows four historical periods. It starts with the New Democratic Revolution, when the concept of intra-Party regulations was first put forward. It then covers socialist revolution and construction, reform and opening up, and finally the new era after the 18th Party Congress (2012). Chi draws on Party constitutions, regulations, and statements by Mao Zedong, Zhu De, Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Hu Jintao and Xi Jinping.

Chi's account is of cumulative development. Before 1949, Party constitutions and regulations, such as those adopted in 1938 and the 1945 Seventh Congress constitution, established democratic centralism and rules for leadership bodies. After 1949, the Eighth Congress (1956) made specific arrangements for collective leadership. Chi concedes, however, that no broad consensus or lasting mechanism took shape across the Party. After 1978, Deng Xiaoping stressed that institutional questions are fundamental and long-term, and by the turn of the century institution-building was formally part of the overall layout of Party building. Since 2012, the author reports, there are over 3,600 Party regulations in force (as of July 2021), covering all levels and categories. Chi also lists the "seven focuses" guiding their improvement.

Chi concludes that ideological and organisational Party building must be combined with institutional governance, with political discipline as the priority. Chi calls institutional governance the Party's "unique code" and claims that it offers a useful reference for party governance and political civilisation worldwide. Read the original if you want a concise, officially framed chronology of how Party-regulation building is presented in Chinese Party-building discourse as of 2022.
quoteEn: Governing the Party through institutions is the Chinese Communist Party's unique code, reflecting the self-confidence, self-reflection and self-reliance of a responsible major party that has endured for a century.
quoteZh: 制度治党是中国共产党的独特密码，体现出一个负责任大党延续百年的自信、自省与自力

glossary.explanation: A concept in Party-building discourse that stresses managing the Party through formal intra-Party rules and regulations, alongside ideological and organisational Party building.
The body of formal rules issued by the Party, including the Party constitution, guidelines, regulations and measures, which bind Party organisations and members.
The Leninist organisational principle of the Party, combining discussion and election with unified discipline and subordination of lower to higher levels.

t: Excellent Chinese etiquette culture should be integrated into the cultivation of core values
zh: 中华优秀礼仪文化应融入核心价值观培育进程
paras: Writing in the Chinese Social Sciences Today in July 2022, Han Yunzhong asks how traditional Chinese etiquette culture can help root the core socialist values in everyday life. The author argues that etiquette and values are inherently consistent and mutually dependent, so that passing on the best of etiquette culture should be built into the cultivation of the core socialist values.

The short commentary first defines traditional etiquette culture and shows that it already carries values such as harmony, civility, good faith and friendliness. It then explains the distinctive role etiquette plays in nurturing values, and ends with four practical routes for linking etiquette to the core socialist values.

Han argues that etiquette has long shaped and transmitted values: coming-of-age, marriage, funeral, village-drinking and court rites each convey particular virtues, internalised as belief and externalised as conduct. Because rites cover every stage of life, they make abstract values visible and tangible and win emotional assent. Citing Xi Jinping on values as a form of virtue, Han holds that etiquette is the outward form of morality, so it promotes moral behaviour.

Han calls for a Marxist-guided, creative transformation of etiquette that discards outdated elaborate ritual. The four routes are education, environmental influence through ceremonies and festivals, family traditions and instructions, and institutional norms such as citizens' pacts, village rules and codes of conduct. Read the original if you want a concise example of how the core socialist values are linked to traditional ritual culture in Chinese public discourse.
quoteEn: Etiquette culture can make abstract value ideas concrete and vivid, helping values enter the mind and the heart.
quoteZh: 礼仪文化能将抽象的价值理念具象化、形象化，推动价值观入脑入心。

glossary.explanation: A twelve-word official set of values (prosperity, democracy, civility, harmony, freedom, equality, justice, rule of law, patriotism, dedication, integrity, friendship) promoted since the 18th Party Congress (2012) at national, social and individual levels.
The moral tone and customs handed down within a family, often expressed in family instructions (jiaxun). Official discourse has encouraged them as a basis for moral education.

t: Mao Zedong's methodological characteristics in advancing the "Two Integrations"
zh: 毛泽东在推进“两个结合”中的方法论特质
paras: How did Mao Zedong's thought emerge from the integration of Marxism with Chinese realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture? Peng Bingbing argues that this integration, which the article calls the Two Integrations, did not happen spontaneously. It required the conscious subjectivity and methodological awareness of Marxist theorists. The article identifies three methodological traits in Mao's practice and presents them as essential for grasping the core of Mao Zedong Thought and for taking the Two Integrations further.

Published in Mao Zedong Thought Studies in 2022, the article is organised in four parts. Three main sections each take up one trait, quoting a phrase of Mao's as a heading: problem awareness and theory-building, the scientific system and its national form, and the people as subject together with mass-oriented discourse. A short conclusion links them to the unity of worldview and methodology. Peng draws on Mao's investigations, his texts from the 1920s to the 1940s, and classical statements by Marx and Engels.

First, theory starts from real problems found through investigation. Peng traces Mao's founding of a Russian studies society (1920), his Hunan peasant report (1927), his rural surveys and his 1930 dictum that without investigation there is no right to speak. Mao's later "seeking truth from facts" line is read as a synthesis of Marxist principle and Chinese tradition, centred on the overall question "where is China headed?". Second, Marxism must take a national form with "Chinese style and Chinese manner". Peng points to Mao's 1938 call to make Marxism concrete in China, his recasting of traditional concepts such as knowing and doing, and his dialectics of contradiction. Third, the people are the subject of history. Peng links this to Mao's mass line and to his use of vivid popular idiom, noting a count of over 2,000 set expressions in the first four volumes of the Selected Works.

Peng concludes that the worldview and methodology of Marxism must be unified in practice, which happens only when theory is made concrete. Because Marxist philosophy is a practical philosophy oriented to the activity of the people, the author holds that adapting Marxism to Chinese conditions must continually address problems that concern the masses. Its results must take national forms and a popular style. On this basis the article calls the sinicization, contemporisation and popularisation of Marxism internally unified. Read the original if you study Mao Zedong Thought, Marxism's adaptation to Chinese conditions, or how Chinese scholars derive method from Mao's practice.
quoteEn: Problem awareness is the subjective, self-conscious awareness behind the development of Marxism, and a basic requirement for every Marxist and Marxist theorist.
quoteZh: 问题意识是马克思主义发展的主体自觉意识，是每一位马克思主义者和马克思主义理论家的基本要求。

glossary.explanation: Formula for combining the basic tenets of Marxism with China's concrete realities and with fine traditional Chinese culture. The second integration was added to the official formulation in 2021–2023.
The Party's official term for the first major theoretical result of adapting Marxism-Leninism to China, formally written into the Party constitution in 1945.
An ideological line, drawn from classical Chinese usage and reinterpreted by Mao in Yan'an, requiring policy to proceed from actual conditions.

Mao's method of leadership in which the Party gathers the views of the masses, concentrates them into policy and then returns to the masses to implement it. The Party adopted it as a fundamental line in 1945.

t: Mao Zedong's thought on adult mass education in the revolutionary base areas during the New Democratic Revolution
zh: 论新民主主义革命时期毛泽东在根据地的成人民众教育思想
source: Mao Zedong Thought Studies (Mao Zedong sixiang yanjiu), 2022 no. 4
paras: The article asks how Mao Zedong's thinking on educating the adult rural population took shape in the Communist-led base areas, and what it achieved. Ren and Du argue that adult education, built on literacy campaigns, was essential for mobilising peasants for revolutionary war. In their account it also left lasting experience for adult education in the People's Republic and in the present.

The authors begin with the background: after 1927 the Party moved its centre of gravity to the countryside, where the base areas were poor, remote and overwhelmingly illiterate. They cite Xu Teli and Li Weihan on illiteracy of 95 to 99 per cent in the north-west. They then set out the content of Mao's ideas in two periods, the Soviet areas of the land revolution era and the Shaan-Gan-Ning base area during the War of Resistance against Japan. Next they review practice and results, and close with lessons for today.

The central argument is that Mao tied education directly to the needs of war. In the Soviet areas the task was to eradicate illiteracy, raise class consciousness and give men and women equal educational rights. During the anti-Japanese war the stated aim became education that served a protracted war. The authors describe three channels of practice: literacy groups, night schools and winter schools; Lenin rooms, libraries and people's education centres, including the blackboard newspaper; and revolutionary folk songs and yangge and Qinqiang performances. They cite statistics, such as the figure that women made up 69 per cent of Xingguo night-school students, to claim lower illiteracy, better hygiene awareness and stronger collective and patriotic consciousness. In their reading, peasants thereby became a reserve force for the army and the war effort.

The authors conclude that this experience opened a path of educational development suited to China's conditions, and that night schools, literacy groups and winter schools later became standard methods of adult education after 1949. For the present they propose linking adult education to production and daily life, encouraging technical training to ease skills shortages, and adding practical courses to compulsory and higher education. They also call for adult education guided by Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era and spread through websites, apps, film and television. Read the original if you want a source-based overview of base-area literacy and mass-education methods, and of how Chinese scholars link them to current adult-education policy.
quoteEn: The night schools, literacy groups, community-run schools and winter schools carried out under the guidance of Mao Zedong's thought on adult mass education became some of the main methods the Chinese Communist Party used for adult education after the founding of the People's Republic.
quoteZh: 在毛泽东成人民众教育思想指导下实行的夜校、识字组、民办学校、冬学等教育方式，成为中国共产党在新中国成立以后开展成人教育的一些主要方式

glossary.zh: 习近平新时代中国特色社会主义思想
glossary.pinyin: Xí Jìnpíng xīn shídài Zhōngguó tèsè shèhuì zhǔyì sīxiǎng
glossary.en: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era
glossary.explanation: The Party's official guiding ideology, written into the Party and state constitutions in 2017–2018. Articles invoke it as the leading framework for current policy.

Rural territories under Communist control, used as bases for armed struggle and administration. They include the Jiangxi Soviet area of the 1930s and the Shaan-Gan-Ning Border Region in the 1937–1945 war.
Seasonal classes held in the slack winter months, when peasants had free time. In the Shaan-Gan-Ning area they taught literacy, hygiene and wartime skills.

t: Revering China's fine traditional culture
zh: 敬仰中华优秀传统文化
paras: This short commentary, published in the People's Daily in July 2022, takes up Xi Jinping's call during an inspection in Sichuan to revere China's fine traditional culture and strengthen cultural confidence. Cai Wencheng argues that national strength rests on cultural flourishing and that the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation requires the development and prosperity of Chinese culture.

The piece moves through four steps, each anchored in quotations from Xi Jinping. It treats culture as a force for national survival, describes the content of fine traditional culture, considers its role amid global upheaval, and links it to the Party's path of Chinese modernization.

Cai contends that China's civilisation, which the author calls the only one in the world to have continued without interruption, sustained the nation through hardship. Fine traditional culture, in this account, carries the nation's "roots and soul" and helps people form correct views of history, nation, state and culture. Cai says that in an era of what the article calls changes unseen in a century and a pandemic, the Party must hold to Marxism, a Chinese cultural standpoint and openness to foreign cultures. The author adds that the Party succeeded because it combined Marxism with China's specific realities and with its fine traditional culture.

Cai concludes that the Chinese Communist Party has taken root in Chinese culture and that contemporary social change offers scope for the creative transformation and innovative development of tradition. The author calls for giving this heritage new value through the practice of socialism with Chinese characteristics in the new era. Read the original if you want a concise example of how official commentary presents cultural confidence and the Two Integrations in 2022.
quoteEn: To revere China's fine traditional culture is to carry it forward in light of new conditions of the times, build Chinese spirit, Chinese values and Chinese strength, and supply inexhaustible spiritual impetus for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.
quoteZh: 敬仰中华优秀传统文化，就要结合新的时代条件传承和弘扬中华优秀传统文化，更好构筑中国精神、中国价值、中国力量，为实现中华民族伟大复兴提供不竭精神动力。

glossary.en: the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation
